activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
The living room smelled like burned nachos and radiator dust, and by halftime the whole party had rearranged itself around Sadie's grandfather, who was holding court from the good armchair with a paper plate balanced on his knee. Sadie sat on the floor between Kiara and the coffee table, close enough to the chip bowl to defend it, while Catherine perched on the arm of the couch pretending to watch the game.

"First one ever," the grandfather was saying. "I was there. Los Angeles, January the fifteenth, 1967. Packers against the Chiefs. Forty below, we nearly froze."

Kiara leaned over and whispered, "Isn't the Super Bowl always indoors or somewhere warm?"

Sadie had been half-listening, the way she listened to most of his stories, filing them between the ones that were true and the ones that were beautiful. She pulled out her phone under the table. Ms. Sánchez, her history teacher, had a rule about this, which was to check primary sources, but Sadie's version was lazier: she typed it into the search bar and waited for the screen to load.

The stadium had been in Los Angeles. That part held. The date held too, January 15, 1967, and the teams were right. The Packers had won, thirty-five to ten. But Los Angeles in January, and forty below, did not belong in the same sentence, and something else snagged her: in 1967 her grandfather would have been nineteen, working, he always said, at his uncle's shop in Ohio. He had told that story too, the winter he couldn't leave the shop because the roads froze. She had heard both versions her whole life and never set them side by side.

"It's a good game," Catherine said from the couch, loudly, the way you say something when you want a different conversation to start.

"Thirty-five to ten," the grandfather said. "People forget how bad it was. Second half, they just folded." He was looking at the screen, but Sadie could tell he was looking at something farther away, something that had the shape of a memory even if it didn't have its facts. He had been sick in the fall. He walked slower now. She had read somewhere that muscles atrophy fast when you stop using them, and she had started to wonder whether the past worked the same way, whether a story left unexercised for fifty years thinned out and something else grew in the space.

She could say it. It would take one sentence: Los Angeles doesn't get forty below, and you were in Ohio, weren't you? Kiara was already watching her, waiting to see which Sadie would show up, because there were two of them and everyone at school knew both. There was the one who won arguments, who kept score, and the one who let things go soft. Her mother called it contrarian; Ms. Sánchez, once, after a class debate about whether it was always wrong to lie, had called it a dialectic, two sides pushing against each other until something truer squeezed out between them. Sadie had liked that word. It made her sound like a process instead of a problem.

But the thing squeezed out between her two sides tonight was not a clean answer. The truth was she couldn't prove he hadn't been in Los Angeles. People crossed state lines in 1967; uncles' shops had other employees. What she could prove was that the weather was wrong, and the wrong weather made the whole thing feel borrowed, maybe from a highlight reel, maybe from a friend who really had gone. The putative memory, the one everyone at this party would now carry as fact because he had said it twice, was already out of his hands and into theirs.

"Grandpa," she said. "Was it really forty below in Los Angeles?"

He looked at her. The room had gone quieter than she wanted, the TV crowd noise filling in behind them.

"Cold enough," he said.

"That's not what I asked."

He set the paper plate down on the armrest. "You know what I remember best? The score. Thirty-five to ten. Old man next to me kept saying it's over, it's over, and I kept saying not yet." He picked the plate back up, took a chip, crunched it. "You check everything on that phone of yours?"

"Almost everything."

"Almost," he said, and almost smiled.

On the screen somebody fumbled and Catherine shouted, and Kiara pulled Sadie back down toward the chip bowl, and the grandfather went on watching the game from wherever he was sitting. Sadie slid the phone into her pocket, screen still warm, the search still open like a door she had decided, for now, to stand in.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In the UK Parliament, a government bill's first reading is a formality: the bill is introduced without debate or a vote.
story:
I am not dramatic about it, but the field trip had been a humiliation, and I told everyone I was fine. Three hours on a coach to Westminster, two forms to fill in, one vending machine that ate Chiara's pound coin, and then the thing we had actually come for: a government bill's first reading, which was over before I had finished unwrapping my sandwich. I swear I described it to my mother as "about forty-five seconds," and she nodded as though that were interesting, and I let her believe I had witnessed something.

It was Chloe who set me straight, in Mr. Oliveira's classroom the next morning, while he handed back our Youth Parliament briefs. "It's a formality," she said. "A government bill's first reading is introduced without debate or a vote. That's the whole point of it. It basically just exists now." She said this the way she said everything, flat and certain, and I hated her a little for having read the booklet on the coach while I was eating. "It lasted, what, seconds?"

"Fine," I said. "Seconds. It was still a waste of a trip."

"It wasn't," Chiara said, but she was already turning to her phone, so I let it go.

Here is what I actually did that evening, at my desk with the lamp on and my laptop open: I started drafting a bill for the Youth Parliament debate, which Mr. Oliveira had assigned as the assessment, and which I had told him I would probably not bother with. My bill concerned bus fares for sixteen-to-eighteen-year-olds in our county, because I had spent two terms paying adult price to get to school while younger students rode half fare, and no one had ever been able to tell me why. I wrote the title, then the clauses, then deleted the clauses, then rewrote them shorter. Clause 1: the county council shall cap fares at the under-sixteen rate for all enrolled students. Clause 2: funding. Clause 2 was the problem. The council's budget was not munificent to begin with, and every time I proposed taking money from somewhere, I could hear the coach, who taught us economics, asking me whose route I was cutting to pay for mine.

I texted Chiara, because she was better at this kind of arithmetic and because Chloe would have made me feel stupid. She came over with her own laptop and we sat on my bed with the pages of drafting between us, arguing about whether the bill should be phased in or whole. "If you phase it, they can claim victory without funding it properly," she said. "If you don't, the committee stage will gut it."

"Then I want it gutted in committee, not in secret," I said, and I meant it, mostly. I had decided, somewhere between the trip and the drafting, that the slowness I had mocked in Westminster was not the same as nothing happening. The formality was a door. The bill walked through the door in seconds and then spent weeks being pulled apart in committee, and if I was honest with myself, that was the part I actually wanted: a room where somebody had to defend the fare cap to my face.

I will admit I nearly faked the rest. The Youth Parliament rules asked each of us to submit a short report on how our bill would move through the stages, and I had planned to copy the structure from the parliamentary website and change the nouns. Instead, at midnight, I read it properly: introduction, committee, report, third reading, votes in both chambers, then royal assent, and at every stage a place where the thing could die. I sat with that for a while. I had been telling people I understood politics since I was about fourteen, which was a lie, and the lie had been comfortable, and I did not feel absolved of it just because I had finally read five pages of procedure.

The debate was on a Thursday, in the hall, with Mr. Oliveira as Speaker. Chloe spoke against my clause 2 with a spreadsheet, which was nearly unanswerable, and the committee of classmates voted to halve the cap. I stood there furious for a second and then thought: this is the room. This is the room I wanted. When they took the final vote, my gutted, halved, phased-in bill passed, eleven to nine, and Chiara leaned across the aisle and whispered that Mr. Oliveira would have to grant it assent now, he had no choice, he'd said so at the start.

He stood, raised his little brass bell, and said, "Be it enacted."

I wrote to my county councillor the same night, at the same desk, and pasted the amended text below a short paragraph about the bus route. At the bottom I typed, "I know this is only a school debate," and then deleted it, and pressed send.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of x to the power n is x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1, for every n except negative 1.
story:
Grandmother's kitchen table had one bad leg, so every time Sara wrote too hard the salt shaker migrated an inch toward the window, and the window looked out on a yard where Grandfather was attempting, at eighty-one, to teach a rescue dog to fetch. Sara had spread her calculus notes across half the table and her lunch across the other half, which Grandmother had already declared a problem in its own right.

"You'll get crumbs in the graph paper," Grandmother said, sliding a plate under the sandwich as if catching it mid-crime. "Then you'll integrate the crumbs."

"Probably," Sara said. She was trying to. College started in five weeks, and the placement exam was in three, and somewhere between the end of junior year and now she had let the whole second half of calculus dissolve out of her head. The house was where she came to remember things. It smelled like laundry and pencil shavings and the particular silence of a place where two old people had worn grooves into their routines.

The topic of the day was area under a curve. Her review book showed a smooth arc with the region beneath it shaded gray, and beside it a formula that lifted the exponent up by one and divided by the new exponent. She copied it onto a fresh sheet. The antiderivative of x to the power n is x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1, for every n except negative 1. She'd underlined the exception twice without thinking, the way you underline something a teacher says with her voice raised.

Her phone buzzed against the table. It was the math club group chat, which she'd never left even after graduating, mostly for the company. Adria had posted a photo of the whiteboard from school, where some junior had tried the rule on one over x and gotten a spectacular mess. Jadyn had replied with a single row of exclamation points and the message "he divided by zero and you could hear it." Sara laughed out loud, and Grandmother looked over with the particular suspicion of a woman who did not trust anything funny that arrived by phone.

"What," Grandmother said, not quite a question.

"Someone at my old school divided by zero," Sara said. "On purpose. Sort of on purpose." She set the phone down and pulled her own sheet closer. One over x was just x to the power negative 1, and the rule said negative 1 was the one exponent it didn't cover. She hadn't believed that kind of thing as a freshman, exceptions. Rules that worked everywhere except exactly one place had seemed like adults hedging. Now she looked at the shaded gray region under the curve and thought about how the area just piled up faster and faster as you approached zero, like the dog in the yard, who had decided that the tennis ball was fine where it was and Grandfather was the one who kept moving.

She tried the arithmetic anyway, because she was her father's daughter. Negative 1 plus 1 was zero, and there was nothing to divide by, and the whole structure folded up flat, exactly the way the kid at school had discovered in front of ten people. She wrote "every n except negative 1" a second time, in the margin, in ink.

Ms. Li from next door knocked at four, holding a rhubarb pie and her own opinions. She was the kind of neighbor who treated an open door as an invitation and a closed door as a challenge. "I saw your grandfather chasing that animal," she announced, setting the pie down on Sara's notes with total confidence. "The dog is winning."

"The dog is winning," Grandmother agreed. They cut the pie immediately, before dinner, which Sara pointed out was basically hedonism, and Ms. Li said that at her age pie before dinner was not indulgence, it was scheduling. Ms. Li asked what Sara was studying, and Sara turned the notebook so she could see the curve and the gray shading, and tried to explain it as the accumulation of little slices, and Ms. Li listened with her chin propped on her hand the way people listen when they actually are listening.

"So you find how much is under it," Ms. Li said. "The whole of what collected."

"The whole of what collected," Sara said. Something about hearing it put that plainly sat differently than the formula had. She'd been treating the exam as a memory problem, but the formula wasn't a fact to memorize, it was two ways of seeing the same shape, and one of them, the picture way, had come to her only now, through a neighbor and a dog and a pie. She was honest enough with herself to admit she still couldn't have said why negative 1 was forbidden, only that it was, and that the forbidden thing had a real shape, a curve that climbed without gathering itself into anything you could total. The gap didn't scare her the way it would have last year. It felt more like a door with a label on it.

Adria texted again: a photo of the whiteboard now wiped clean, with the message "we told him it happens to everyone." Sara sent back "tell him it happened to me today too, at a kitchen table, with a witness." She held the phone up so Ms. Li and Grandmother could see the thread, and Ms. Li read it and snorted into her coffee, and Grandmother said, "Salt," and nudged the shaker back toward the center of the table with one finger, the way she'd been doing for forty years.

Sara picked her pen back up and started the next problem in the book, but she pulled the shaded drawing closer first, the drawing and not the formula, and she began at the left edge of the gray region, at the small end where everything was still polite.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Ireland's Great Famine began in 1845 when potato blight struck a population that relied heavily on one potato variety, the Lumper, whose lack of genetic variety left it vulnerable.
story:
Levi had promised Ria he would have an answer by Saturday, and now it was Friday afternoon and the library's heating was making the window beside him too warm to lean against. The answer was supposed to be about the community garden plot behind the mosque on Alder Street, the one their class had been granted after two years of petitions. Forty metres of south-facing soil, and a decision: what to plant, and how many kinds, and who would decide. Ria wanted beans, a single reliable row of them, because beans had produced last year at her grandmother's plot and because everyone on the street would actually eat them. Rachel had argued for eleven different vegetables, half of which nobody in the neighbourhood cooked with, on the grounds that variety was its own kind of virtue. Levi had been given the job of finding evidence, because both of them claimed they were too busy, and because he was the one who had wanted the garden in the first place.

He spread his materials across the table: a county extension pamphlet on soil testing, a printout of seed costs from the hardware store two neighbourhoods over where the prices were lower, and a borrowed history with a cracked spine, Ms. Iyer's own copy, which she had pressed into his hands that morning when he'd admitted what the argument was about. "Look at chapter nine," she had said, and nothing more, which was her way. She taught like someone who believed that handing you the right door was enough and that opening it yourself was the part that mattered.

Chapter nine was about Ireland. Levi read the first page expecting battle dates and instead got fields, and a single potato variety called the Lumper. He read it twice. The Lumper was what the population relied on, the book said, and when the blight came in 1845, the lack of genetic variety in that one crop left the whole country exposed to it. A population leaning on a single dependable thing, and a disease that knew exactly where to look. He sat with that for a moment, aware of a faint presentiment, some part of him already assembling the parallel before he had decided whether he trusted it.

He got up to find Ria, who was supposed to be shelving returns in the 600s but was instead sitting on the floor behind the cart, scrolling through her phone. She looked up when he crouched beside her.

"Did you know," he said, keeping his voice down, "the Irish famine started with one kind of potato? The Lumper. Everyone grew it, everyone ate it, and when blight hit in 1845 there was nothing to fall back on, because one variety meant no genetic variety at all. The whole thing went at once."

Ria's thumb stopped moving. "Beans," she said, not as a question.

"Beans," Levi agreed. "Or beans plus other things."

She stood up, dusted her knees, and followed him back to the table, which felt like a small victory until she sat down and pushed the seed printout toward him with two fingers. "Look at the prices, though. The bean seed is a third of anything else. My mum can chip in for beans. She can't chip in for eleven vegetables, and Rachel's family is moving, did she tell you that? Probably not. End of the month."

Levi hadn't known. Rachel's mother had been the one with the car who drove the water barrels to the plot in August, the one who had signed the petition first, and now the family was leaving, which meant the garden was losing a pair of hands and Rachel was losing something he couldn't price. He thought of her argument for eleven vegetables differently now: not as a love of variety for its own sake, some extrinsic principle she'd read about, but as a way of saying she wanted the garden to hold as many people as possible, to be a thing with room in it.

"Her mum's the one with the compost setup," he said.

"And the hose connection. And the Saturday mornings." Ria pulled the history book toward her and turned to chapter nine herself, reading in the rapid way she read when she was looking for ammunition rather than understanding. He watched her arrive at the paragraph about the Lumper and watched her face change from calculation to something quieter. She closed the book gently, which for Ria was a kind of concession.

"So we plant beans," she said, "and something else. Two or three things. Not because Rachel wants eleven."

"Because the Lumper," Levi said, and she nodded.

They found Rachel in the periodicals section, pretending to do her history essay, and Levi laid it out for her: the cost problem, the hands problem, the single-crop problem, 1845, all of it, and then the compromise he had been assembling in his head since the floor of the 600s. Beans as the spine of the garden, three reliable rows, plus squash along the fence because it was cheap and heavy-yielding, plus whatever seed packets people on the street wanted to bring themselves, so the variety came from the neighbourhood rather than from a catalogue. Not eleven. Not one. Rachel listened with her chin on her fist, and when he finished she said, "You knew about the moving?"

"My mum told your mum at the market," Levi said.

Rachel looked at the window for a while, at the wet street and the bus shelter and the grey light coming off everything. "I'll come back for harvest," she said. "Even if we're in Mississauga. I'll take the bus." Then she reached across and pulled the seed printout toward her, found a pen in her bag, and started crossing things out, and Ria leaned over her shoulder to argue about the squash, and Levi sat back and let them fight about it, because there were things he was still unsure of, like whether three crops was actually enough or whether enough was even the right question for a piece of dirt nobody had tested yet, and because some decisions you could only instantiate by putting seeds in the ground and waiting through a season to see what came up.

Ria circled one line on the printout and tapped it twice with the pen. "Saturday," she said. "Nine o'clock. Bring the book."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA recommends eating refrigerated cooked leftovers within three to four days, which limits how far ahead a week of meals can be cooked without freezing some.
story:
Hannah stood at the steel counter in the back of Ms. Patel's restaurant kitchen, six empty containers lined up in front of her like exam booklets before a test she hadn't studied for. Ms. Patel had agreed to let her use the kitchen on Sunday afternoons, when the restaurant was closed, on the condition that Hannah leave everything cleaner than she found it. Hannah had the whole plan written on a folded sheet of notebook paper: Sunday cooking, seven lunches, one for each day of the week at college, because the dining hall cost more than her scholarship covered and the vending machine diet of her first semester had been, in her mother's careful word, deleterious.

"Seven," said Evie, reading over her shoulder. Evie had come to help, or possibly to eat. "That's ambitious."

"It's arithmetic," Hannah said. "Cook once, eat all week. My aunt does it."

Ms. Patel came through the swinging door carrying a crate of onions she was letting Hannah use at cost. She was a quiet woman who ran her kitchen the way Hannah's English teacher ran a seminar: nothing announced, everything noticed. When Hannah explained the plan, all seven containers, all cooked today, all refrigerated, Ms. Patel slowed her wiping of the counter and looked at the lineup for a long moment.

"You're going to eat number seven when?" she asked.

"Next Saturday," Hannah said.

"And you cooked it today."

Hannah said yes, and waited, because Ms. Patel's questions were rarely really questions. Ms. Patel didn't answer either. She went back to her onions and let the silence do its work, which was, Hannah would think later, the most teacherly thing she'd ever seen anyone do in a kitchen.

Hannah pulled out her phone and looked it up herself, because that was how she'd rather learn things anyway. There it was on the USDA page: eat refrigerated cooked leftovers within three to four days. She read it twice, then a third time, doing the count on her fingers against the steel counter like a child. If she cooked on Sunday, day four was Wednesday, maybe Thursday at the outside. Saturday's lunch wasn't a week of meals. It was a science experiment in a container. She stood there with the phone in one hand and her whole beautiful plan in the other, feeling the specific humiliation of someone who had been proud of an idea that turned out to be half an idea.

"So the last ones go in the freezer," Evie said, peering at the screen.

"But then they're not really batch leftovers, they're frozen meals," Hannah said, and heard how petty it sounded the moment it left her mouth. Evie raised an eyebrow. Hannah laughed, which was not what she'd planned to do. "Fine. Days one to four in the fridge, days five to seven in the freezer. Thursday night I move Friday's down to thaw. It's not the plan I had. It's a different plan."

"Congratulations," Evie said. "You've reinvented the freezer."

Ms. Patel, still at her onions, made a sound that was almost a laugh. She had declined all along to lecture, but she did tell Hannah one thing while the rice was on: that she herself cooked in batches twice a week, not once, and had for twenty years, and that Hannah could predicate a whole sane week on that rhythm if she wanted to. Twice a week meant nothing sat more than a few days. Hannah turned this over while she browned the ground turkey, thinking that her original plan had been built on an assumption she'd never checked, and that the corrected plan required more work, not less, and that this was probably true of most things.

They cooked until six. Hannah portioned four containers into the fridge and three into the restaurant's chest freezer, labeled with grease pencil in her small, deliberate handwriting: Thu, Fri, Sat. She had wanted the week to be a single solved problem, one afternoon of effort exchanged for seven days of ease, and instead it was a rhythm, a thing you kept doing. Evie ate a bowl of the turkey and rice standing up and pronounced Hannah a true gourmand, which was generous given that the recipe had come off a library printer and involved exactly five ingredients. Hannah scrubbed the steel counter until it showed her reflection, hung the towel to dry, and carried the notebook paper plan out with her, the word FREEZER now written across Thursday in block letters so large it bent the margin.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Test-driven development, popularized by Kent Beck, follows a 'red, green, refactor' cycle: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code.
story:
Liam opened his laptop at his grandfather's kitchen table, between a bowl of tomatoes still warm from the garden and a crossword folded to the sports page. The assignment from the summer camp had arrived that morning: build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods, then test it. He had assumed the testing part would come last, the way you check a cake after it's baked. The email said otherwise. Write the test first, it said. Before the class exists.

He called Milana, who was doing the same camp from her aunt's house two towns over. "That's the point," she said, her voice tinny through his phone's speaker. "It's called test-driven development. Kent Beck popularized it." She held her own screen up to the camera for a second, a blur of red underlines. "You write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code. Red, green, refactor. My test doesn't even compile right now because there's nothing to test."

"That's like grading a test before the student exists," Liam said.

"Sure, if the student is imaginary and you get to invent him afterward."

He hung up, still doubtful, and started typing. It felt wrong the way rowing a boat backward feels wrong at first, all the oars in the wrong place. His grandfather came through with a watering can and paused behind him. "Your grandmother used to write the recipe title first," the old man said, "before she'd cooked a thing. Said a dish without a name was just ingredients arguing." Liam filed that away, unsure whether it was wisdom or just something a man says to keep his hands busy while he waters porch plants.

The flashback arrived on its own. In the spring, Ms. Kim had made them write lab conclusions before doing the experiments, and he'd thought it was a trick, some exercise in being wrong on purpose. He'd written that the plants with more light would grow taller, and they had, mostly, except for the one pot by the window vent that had shriveled. Ms. Kim had circled his prediction and written, "Good guess. Now what did you control?" At the time it had felt like criticism. Sitting here now, with an empty file and a test demanding a class called Plant that didn't exist yet, it felt more like a door he'd walked past.

He wrote the test: create a Plant, set its height and its name through the constructor, ask for the values back. The compiler refused it, red everywhere, because Plant was nothing. That was apparently the red part, and it was strange to feel satisfied by failure, like a doctor glad the test came back positive for the disease she suspected. Then he built the class, small and careful: private fields, height and name hidden away where nobody could reach in and change them by accident, and two getter methods, plain little doors that let information out without letting chaos in. The test went green. He actually said "ha" out loud, alone in the kitchen, and the cat on the windowsill gave him a look that suggested it had heard better.

His summer homework for college bio was open in another tab, a diagram about genotype and phenotype, and it struck him that the class worked the same way. The private fields were the genotype, hidden instructions inside; the getters were the traits the world could actually observe. Nobody shook hands with your DNA. They shook hands with your height, your diurnal tendency to be either awake at breakfast or a zombie until noon, the things your insides had decided to show. And the test came before the code the way the phenotype couldn't exist without something underneath it, asking to be expressed.

The refactor step was the one he'd have skipped if the email hadn't spelled it out. Make it pass, then clean up the code. He looked at what he'd written, which worked but was ugly, the variable names improvised, one getter doing a small unnecessary calculation it didn't need to do. He understood, sitting there, that he was holding two ideas that didn't quite subsume each other: his old instinct, that you build first and check after, and this newer one, that the checking is the design. He couldn't say yet which was really better, or whether they were opposites at all or just two ends of the same habit of mind. Ms. Kim would probably say he hadn't controlled for anything.

He cleaned up the code anyway, renamed a variable, ran the test again, and watched it stay green. In the garden his grandfather moved between the tomato rows with the unhurried patience of someone who had planted things and then waited, which was maybe the oldest version of the whole idea. Liam took a tomato from the bowl, turned it over once in his hand, and typed, "Works. How far did you get?"

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
story:
Charlie spread the briefs across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with salt shakers because the porch door kept letting in a draft. The house smelled of cardamom and old paper, and her grandmother moved around her with tea and sliced pear, saying nothing for a full hour, which Charlie understood as a kind of generosity. In two days she would stand before a mock court of teachers and lawyers and argue both sides of a case about speech: the same angry speech, first as the state of Ohio defending a conviction, then as the speaker demanding his freedom. Her grandmother's table was the only place big enough to hold the whole argument at once.

She had written the government's half first, and it had come easily, almost suspiciously so. The speech was real, quoted in the record: a man at a rally, contemptuous of certain citizens, declaring that revenge was a possibility and that if it should come, so much the better. Charlie had drafted four paragraphs about order and fear before Mr. Ramos, her coach for the competition, had read the draft and slid it back across his desk. "You've argued that the speech is ugly," he said. "Nobody disputes that. Find me the rule." He would not say more, which was his method and, Charlie suspected, his cruelty and his kindness braided together.

The rule took her most of the evening and one pear to find. It lived in a case called Brandenburg v. Ohio, decided in 1969, and when she read the holding aloud she had to read it twice more, slowly, because every word seemed to be doing deliberate work. The Court had held that advocating force, even advocating revenge and disorder, could be punished only if it was directed to inciting imminent lawless action and was likely to produce such action. She copied it onto an index card. "Imminent," she said to the kitchen, and her grandmother, drying a cup, said, "That word was your grandfather's favorite. He used it to mean Tuesday, usually."

Leia arrived after dinner with her own briefs and a bag of licorice, voluble as always, already halfway through a story about the cashier at the gas station who had strong opinions about the competition. She dropped into the chair opposite Charlie and stole a pear slice without asking, which was their oldest treaty. "I have the same case," she said. "I'm only arguing the speech side. You have to argue both. That's deranged."

"It's the format," Charlie said. "They want to see if you can hold two positions without letting either one desiccate into a slogan." She had learned the word from Mr. Ramos in September and had been waiting all term for a sentence that deserved it.

Leia made her run the government side while Leia heckled from the judges' table, which was really the head of the table where Charlie's grandmother had ruled for forty years. "Why shouldn't the state punish him?" Leia demanded, chewing licorice. "The speech is vile."

Charlie reached for her fear paragraphs and heard herself setting them aside. "Because the test isn't whether it's vile," she said. "Advocating force can be punished only if it's directed to inciting imminent lawless action and it's likely to produce it. He was talking to a rally, in the abstract, about something that might someday happen. Not tonight. Not 'follow me now.' And nobody moved."

"So imminent means soon," Leia said. "Like, right now soon."

"And likely means it would actually work," Charlie said. "Both doors have to open. If the speech isn't aimed at starting something immediately, or if it probably couldn't, the First Amendment closes around it." Leia looked almost betrayed, as if the rule had cheated on her behalf of the government.

That night, unable to sleep in the guest room with its ticking clock, Charlie found a letter her grandfather had written to her mother years ago, folded into the guest drawer where the good paper was kept. He had written it the week her mother left for college, and the last page was about an argument he'd lost on purpose: "Your grandmother wanted the porch painted white and I wanted gray, and I have come to believe I was wrong, not because the white is more beautiful, but because I could not say why I wanted gray without lying a little. Hold your positions loosely, sweetheart. The ones worth keeping survive being argued against." Charlie read it three times, then held it in both hands and let the clock tick.

The next morning her grandmother drove them to the school, and the drive was mostly quiet except for a moment at the light by the river when her grandmother said, "Your grandfather would have paid money to watch this." In the hallway outside the mock courtroom, Leia squeezed Charlie's shoulder and whispered, "Desiccate them," which was not a sentence Charlie could defend in any court.

When the bailiff, who was really a sophomore with a gavel she took too seriously, called the case, Charlie stood and walked to the podium. The panel of three judges looked down at her, and she thought of gray porches, of rallies where nobody moved, of a man whose words were terrible and protected anyway. She took a breath, rested her fingers on the index card, and said, "May it please the court."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, passed over President Truman's veto, allowed US states to pass right-to-work laws banning contracts that require workers to pay union fees.
story:
Lauren had the envelope in her backpack, the one with her new schedule from the grocery store taped inside it, and she had promised herself she would ask Ms. Joseph about it before third period ended. The schedule said her Sunday shifts were now nine hours, with no extra pay, and when she had asked the manager he had shrugged and said everyone's looked like that. She didn't know if that was allowed. She didn't know who to ask.

Ms. Joseph had set the desks in a horseshoe for the simulation. Half the class were "management," half were "workers," and a stack of index cards on the front table assigned each worker a card with a name and a home state. Lauren drew a card that said she had moved to Michigan from Tennessee. Edgar, across the horseshoe, drew Michigan. Megane drew management, which made her morose, because she had wanted to argue the workers' side, and she said so while shuffling her papers.

The negotiation was about a contract for a fictional warehouse. Management offered a wage of eleven dollars an hour. Edgar, playing a shift leader, stood up and said the workers wanted fourteen, overtime after eight hours, and a clause requiring everyone hired to pay union dues. That last item was where everything stopped.

"Wait," Megane said, flipping through her notes. "My cousin works at a plant in Tennessee. She doesn't pay dues and she's still covered by the contract. She said it's the law there."

"That's right," Edgar said. "The Taft-Hartley Act. Nineteen forty-seven. It passed over Truman's veto, and it lets states pass right-to-work laws."

Lauren looked up. "What's a right-to-work law?"

"It bans contracts that require workers to pay union fees," Edgar said. "So in her state nobody has to pay. In Michigan they can be required to."

Lauren wrote it down slowly, because something about it snagged on her. She had moved, in the simulation, from Tennessee to Michigan, and under the card she had stopped being someone who could sit out and started being someone who had to pay. The same worker. Two different rules, depending on the map. She thought of the way her manager had said everyone's schedule looked like that, as if a rule existed somewhere that made it so, and she wondered whether rules like that were written by people or just happened, the way weather happened.

Ms. Joseph was walking the room, saying almost nothing, which Lauren had learned meant the simulation was going the way she wanted. When the workers' caucus met in the corner, Edgar argued that the dues clause had to stay in the contract because without it people would take the benefits and skip the cost, and the union would starve. Another student, playing a worker who had just moved from a right-to-work state, said she resented being forced to pay for something she hadn't voted on. They went back and forth, and Lauren mostly listened, turning her pen over in her fingers, and then she said, "I moved here from Tennessee on my card. Under the old rules I paid nothing. Now I'd pay. But the hours thing, the overtime, the safety stuff, that's what I actually care about. Maybe the dues question is smaller than what the dues buy."

Edgar had been watching Lauren all morning, not just because she was smart, though she was, but because she kept reaching back to touch her backpack like there was something in it she was guarding. When she finally pulled out the envelope and showed it to Megane, who worked at the same grocery store, he understood. Megane read the schedule, and her mouth flattened, and she said, "They did this to the baggers too. My mom said her store did the opposite, actually, cut hours so nobody hits overtime."

"Is there anyone at our store who decides that," Lauren asked, "or does it just come down from somewhere?"

"There's a notice board in the break room," Megane said. "There's a number on it. I never read it."

Edgar watched Lauren copy the number off Megane's phone into her own, carefully, digit by digit, the way someone writes down a thing they intend to use. He thought about telling her that a phone number was a crude heuristic for a whole system of laws, that one call rarely fixed anything, but she already knew that; he could see she knew it, and he could see she was going to call anyway. The dues clause passed in the simulation by one vote, and the right-to-work state got carved out as an exception, which Ms. Joseph said was very close to what had actually happened in places, and then the bell rang.

In the hall, Megane caught up with Lauren and pressed the envelope back into her hands. "Text me when you call the number," she said. "I'll call too. It counts more if it's not just one person."

Lauren slid the envelope into the front pocket of her backpack, where she could feel it against her spine all the way to fourth period.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
The living room had been rearranged so that everyone could see the television, folding chairs pulled in from the kitchen, the good couch surrendered to Grandpa, who had watched hockey in this room since before Laura's mother was born. Natalia arrived first with a bag of chips and no understanding of icing, which she admitted freely, and Maryam came next, having sworn off the sport after her brothers used her as a goalie for an entire childhood. Mr. Henry from next door let himself in at the second intermission, holding a bowl of his wife's seven-layer dip and saying only, "I heard the cheering from my porch."

It was game seven, which Laura understood in her body before she understood it anywhere else. Something about a seventh game made every save feel borrowed, every shot a question with no safe answer. Her mother kept leaving the room to check on the food she wasn't cooking, and Grandpa kept his eyes on the screen the way other people watched a hospital door.

"The trophy's older than this whole country's worst habits," Grandpa announced during a lull, apropos of nothing Laura could see. "Oldest trophy in North American professional sports, and still the same one. They don't retire it and mint a new one like the others do."

Laura, who was texting under a blanket, looked up. "They don't make a new one each year? Like the Lombardi trophy?"

"New one every year for football. Not this. This one gets handed over."

Natalia leaned toward Laura with the particular hunger of someone who has found a fact-shaped hole in a conversation. "How old, though? Actually old, or grandpa old?"

"Look it up yourself," Grandpa said, without turning his head.

She did, thumbing through her phone while the third period started without her. Donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, a governor general, and first awarded in 1893. She read it twice, because 1893 was before her school, before her street, before most of the trees she could name. A hundred and thirty years of men lifting the same silver thing over their heads, and the thing itself had outlasted all of them. She tried to interpolate her own life into that span and couldn't quite manage it; seventeen years sat inside a hundred and thirty like a single shift inside a long game.

"It was first awarded in 1893," she said out loud. "A guy named Lord Stanley of Preston donated it in 1892. Oldest existing trophy for a professional sports team in North America. That's what this says."

"There," Grandpa said, as though she had passed a test he hadn't admitted to giving.

Mr. Henry, who had been quietly assembling a chip with surgical amounts of dip, cleared his throat. "Forgive me, but does it matter? The age. The game in front of us is happening now."

"It matters to me," Laura said, and then, because she was seventeen and honest even when it cost her something, "I'm not entirely sure why. Maybe because tonight either team wins a cup that's been won since 1893, and that makes tonight feel like part of something, instead of just loud. Or maybe I'm being a hedonist about history, collecting old facts because they feel fancy." She heard herself and winced. "That's not the word. A hedonist is about pleasure. I mean I might just like the feeling of knowing things."

"You like the feeling," Maryam said. "We know. You read the Wikipedia page at parties."

The room laughed, and the game tightened, and Grandpa gripped the arm of the good couch with both hands. Laura found herself watching him more than the puck. His whole face was doing the arithmetic of a lifetime of games, some won, most not, and she wondered whether the cup being old meant anything to him personally or whether he simply liked saying so, the way people liked saying a wine was from a good year. Maybe both. Maybe the pithy version, "oldest trophy in North America," and the long true version, all the hands that had held it, were the same fact wearing different clothes, and she could keep both in her head at once without having to choose.

The tying goal came with under four minutes left, and the living room went up in a single hoarse sound, dip nearly lost, Natalia on her feet though she still could not name a single player. In the overtime that followed, nobody spoke. Grandpa's lips moved without sound, and Mr. Henry had stopped eating altogether, and Laura sat with her phone dark in her lap, having decided nothing except that she wanted to be here, in this room, watching this old thing get won.

When the winning goal went in, Grandpa stood up faster than Laura had ever seen him stand, and Maryam grabbed Natalia's arm, and somewhere in the pile of cheering Laura heard her own voice among the others, shouting, "It's the same cup!"

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other.
story:
Luke set his laptop on the kitchen table between his mother's coffee mug and the fruit bowl, opened the assignment page, and read the prompt for the third time. Overlay the city's flood hazard layer on the housing stock layer, the teacher had written, and identify which neighbourhoods sat in the path of a hundred-year flood. Mr. Dhillon had shown them one demo in the lab on Tuesday, his cursor gliding across the projected screen while layers clicked on and off like sheets of glass, and then he had said, with the mild cheerfulness that made even hard assignments feel like invitations, that the rest they would figure out on their own.

The house was quiet except for the refrigerator's hum. Luke's mother was at her shift at the hospital, his father was in the garage sorting boxes for the move they kept postponing, and the late afternoon light came sideways through the window, warming the edge of the table and the rim of the empty mug. He downloaded the flood layer from the provincial site and the housing layer from the city's open data portal, imported both, and clicked them on together for the first time.

The river ran straight through city hall. It cut through the arena, sliced a diagonal across the school where Hussain's little sister went, and pooled improbably in the middle of the industrial park, nowhere near the actual channel he had crossed every morning on the bus for as long as he could remember. He stared at it. Then he laughed once, alone in the kitchen, because the map looked like something a child had drawn, a blue scribble where a building should be. His first thought was that the flood data was garbage. His second thought, slower and more uncomfortable, was that the problem might be him.

He took a screenshot and texted Hussain. Can you check your map. My river goes through city hall. For a minute there was nothing, just the three dots appearing and vanishing, and Luke sat with his hands flat on the table, watching the light move off the fruit bowl. Then the reply came: Mine too. Then, a second message: Roberto says his is normal. His layers line up. Then a third, which Roberto had evidently dictated: Did you use the city portal for both layers? Luke checked. The flood layer was provincial. The housing layer was municipal. They came from two different agencies, two different websites, two different shapes of the same city.

He opened the layer properties the way Mr. Dhillon had shown them, half remembering, half guessing. Somewhere in the metadata there was a field for the coordinate system, and when he found it, the two layers listed different values. He did not understand everything he was looking at, but the difference itself was plain, and it lined up with the only other thing he knew: the layers were stored in different coordinate reference systems, and until one was reprojected to match the other, they would not line up. He typed this into the group chat, hesitated, deleted the second half, and sent only the first part. Hussain replied almost immediately: Reproject. That's the word. Mr. Dhillon said it in the demo, I wrote it down.

The tool took Luke three tries. The first time he reprojected the wrong layer and the river slid even further from where it belonged, ending up in a farmer's field two towns over, and he sat back and pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes for a moment before undoing it. The second time the menu defeated him with its greyed-out options. On the third try the city snapped into place, all at once, the way a word puzzle suddenly reads correctly, and the river flowed along its true channel, past the levee and under the two bridges, and the floodplain spread out around it in pale blue.

He leaned in. The overlay told its story quickly now, and it was not a comforting one. The oldest housing, the narrow lots and flat-roofed walk-ups where Roberto's cousins lived, sat almost entirely inside the hazard zone. The newer subdivisions on the hill, the ones with the landscaped entrances, sat outside it. Luke had read enough arguments about the river to know both the sympathetic version and the scathing one, the version his uncle liked, which held that anyone who built on a floodplain deserved whatever the water did. He was starting to think both versions were too easy, that the map made the situation look like a choice when it might have been anything but.

His father came in for water, saw the screen, and asked what he was looking at. Luke explained it in the plainest words he could, pointing at the blue and the clusters of rooftops beneath it. His father stood with the glass in his hand for longer than a drink of water required. We looked at a house over there, he said finally, before you were born. Didn't buy it. He did not say why, and Luke did not ask, but the sentence stayed in the room after his father went back to the garage.

Luke pulled up the chat one more time. Hussain had sent his own finished map, correctly aligned, with a single message beneath it: So the poor neighbourhoods get the water and the rich ones get the hill. It was the same conclusion Luke had reached, stated without hedge or softening, and he admired it and distrusted it in nearly equal measure, because he could not yet tell from the data whether the pattern held across the whole city or only the part he had zoomed into. There was a note field in the housing layer he had not opened, and a column of construction dates he had not sorted. He zoomed out one level, so that the whole city fit on the screen at once, blue and grey and rooftop-coloured, and began clicking through the parcels one by one, starting at the river.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
The U-Haul arrived before Zoey did, so her first sight of the new house was a ramp of boxes slanting into the garage, and her mother waving from the porch like a woman hailing a rescue. Zoey counted the boxes with her eyes instead of answering. Ninety-three. She had packed most of them herself, and she knew which one held the shoebox of notes she and Priya had passed back and forth through three years of biology, French, and a semester of gym they had both survived by complaining.

On her second morning, she looked up from her cereal and said, "Did you know a researcher figured out how long it takes to make a close friend?" Her mother set down the coffee pot. "Two hundred hours. Jeffrey Hall, 2018. More than two hundred hours spent together." She said it as if reciting the charges against the person who had moved them. Her mother said that was a lot of hours, and Zoey said that was the point, that she had done the math on the drive here. Six hours a day at school, five days a week, thirty-six weeks, three years, minus holidays and sick days, and she was not going to do the subtraction out loud because the total was like a debt.

At the new school, Mr. Nolan had already assigned her a seat in third-period English beside a boy named Dan, who lent her a pen without being asked, which she logged as a small credit in an invisible ledger she had started keeping without quite admitting it. In the hallway a girl named Micah knocked shoulders with her and said sorry and then said, "You're the new one, right? Ohio?" Zoey said yes and then, because the number was sitting right there in her mouth, said, "It takes more than two hundred hours to make a close friend. I read it in a study." Micah blinked. "So we're at, what, four minutes?"

Zoey laughed, and the laugh surprised her, and she didn't write it in the ledger.

She had a plan, because she was that kind of person. The plan was arithmetic. If she spent lunch with Dan and Micah every day, five hours a week, she would reach two hundred hours by spring, which meant spring was when she could stop performing and start being herself, which meant she had to perform for six months. The performing was not hard exactly, but it was tiring the way holding a smile in a photograph for too long is tiring. When Dan told a story about a teacher's peccadillo, the way he mispronounced "colonel" during announcements every single morning, Zoey laughed on cue and wondered whether the real her would have laughed, and whether there was even a difference.

The twist came in November, on the bus back from a debate meet where she and Micah had shared headphones and a bag of pretzels. Micah was scrolling her phone and said, "You know that two hundred hour thing? I looked it up. It's real. Jeffrey Hall, 2018." She turned the screen. Zoey read it in the dark of the bus, the window blurring past streetlights, and felt something in her chest go quiet. "But here's the thing," Micah said. "It says close friends. Like best friends. The study said it takes more than two hundred hours for that. Did you read the part about the middle kind?" There was a middle kind, apparently, friends in the ordinary sense, who took less. Hours Zoey had already stopped counting.

Zoey had been treating the number like a wall between her and everyone here, a fact that proved she was still, technically, alone. She understood slowly, over the next few days, that she had been using it wrong. Priya was not two thousand irreplaceable hours banked in the past; Priya was also a phone call on Sunday that Zoey had skipped twice because calling felt like admitting the distance. The old friendship and the new ones were not opposites, two doors where you could only walk through one. She had been thinking of the hours as bricks, when maybe they were more like weather, something you stood in rather than stacked.

She called Priya that night anyway, her heart hammering like it was the first week of anything. Priya answered on the second ring and said, "Finally," and told a story about their old biology teacher that made Zoey put her hand over her eyes, and the call lasted an hour and forty minutes, which she noticed herself noticing, and then made herself stop noticing. The next day at lunch she sat with Dan and Micah and did not calculate, or mostly did not, and when Dan asked what she was smiling about she said, "Pretzels," which was evanescent, the way the true reasons for things often are, already gone before she finished saying it.

Mr. Nolan stopped her after class on Friday with a form for the spring debate team, and she signed it at his desk, and Micah leaned in the doorway waiting, holding two milks from the vending machine, and said, "Come on, Ohio, bus leaves in ten."

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Particle physicists claim a discovery only at 'five sigma', meaning there is less than a one-in-a-million chance that a random fluctuation alone would produce a signal that strong.
story:
The printout lay flat on the study table between three books Joshua had pulled at random, the way you test whether a floor is level. Seven weeks of lunch periods in the school physics lab, forty-two trials of bean seedlings under different magnetic field strengths, and the difference in germination rates came out to nine percent. Nine percent. The kind of number that could mean something, or could mean nothing at all, and he could not tell which, and the regional science fair was in eleven days.

He had come to the library because the lab made him feel watched, and home made him feel decided, his mother already telling relatives about his project as though the result were a fact rather than a wobble. Here, on the second floor near the periodicals, nobody knew what the numbers meant, including him. He spread the data across the table and stared at it until the decimal points blurred.

"You look like you're reading a will," Alyson said, dropping her bag into the chair opposite. She had finished her own project in October, something about stream acidity, and had been unbearable about it ever since. She leaned over without asking and pulled the printout toward her. "Nine percent. That's a thing, right? That's an effect."

"Or it's noise," Joshua said. "I reran the control group last week and the gap shrank. Then it came back. It breathes."

"That's data being alive."

"That's data being unreliable." He turned his notebook to the page where he'd been sketching confidence intervals, an idea he half remembered from a video and half invented, which was a dangerous ratio. He was spared working out which half when Ms. Yoon appeared at the table's end with a cart of returns, her eyes catching the scatter of numbers the way a birder's catch movement in brush.

Ms. Yoon had, in her own view of the matter, spent thirty-one years watching students mistake enthusiasm for evidence, and she had learned exactly when to intervene, which was almost never. But this one had come to the library instead of the lab, which meant he already doubted himself, which meant he was halfway to being worth helping. She let the cart roll to a stop and set one book on his stack, a collection of essays on the history of measurement that she had been saving for someone. "For the section on uncertainty," she said, and moved on toward the periodicals before he could thank her or, worse, ask her a question she would have to answer.

Alyson found it first, forty minutes later, on page ninety-two, in an interview with a physicist about the discovery of the Higgs boson. She read the passage twice, then held the book open and turned it around. "They waited years to claim it," she said. "Even after the data looked good. Particle physicists claim a discovery only at five sigma."

Joshua took the book. Five sigma, the interview explained, meant there was less than a one-in-a-million chance that a random fluctuation alone would produce a signal that strong. He read the sentence aloud, quietly, then again. Somewhere behind the periodical shelves a printer clattered through a page of somebody's essay.

"One in a million," Alyson said. "Your bean thing is like one in four, maybe. If you're lucky."

"So I have nothing."

"So you have a beginning." She tapped the margin of his notebook, where the failed confidence interval slumped. "You scale up. You write it as, here is a small effect, here is how many trials it would take to be sure, here is why being sure matters. You show the math of doubt."

He looked at the printout, at the nine percent that had seemed, an hour ago, like a verdict. It was strange how the same number could shrink and grow depending on what you demanded of it. His mother would still tell the relatives; he knew that the way you know weather is coming. He could not apportionment the blame between his own vanity and her pride, and the more he thought about it, the less he wanted to, because the apportionment itself felt like another unverified claim. What he could do was run sixty more trials before the fair, log every one, and say exactly how certain he was, which was not very, and then say what it would take.

Alyson had already opened a fresh page in his notebook and written at the top, in her blunt hand, "What would five sigma require?" Under it she began listing: more seeds, more days, a second grow lamp borrowed from the coach whose storage room held everything the school had ever bought and forgotten, sectarian about lending it but persuadable by casseroles. Joshua laughed at that, and she shrugged, and Ms. Yoon, shelving periodicals three rows over, heard the laugh and did not look up, only allowed herself the smallest nod before pushing the cart on toward biography.

Joshua gathered the data sheets into his folder, squared the corners, and checked out the book. At the circulation desk he paused over the due date, then flipped to page ninety-two and folded the corner down, a small crease to underwrite what he was about to spend eleven days chasing.

"One in a million," he said to Alyson as they pushed through the doors into the cold. "Let's go ask the coach about that lamp."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Programmers describe linear search as O(n), meaning its work grows in step with the list, and binary search as O(log n), meaning its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size.
story:
The whiteboard in the library's small study room still said O(log n) in marker when Peyton arrived, left over from whoever had the room before. She had copied it into her notebook during Tuesday's session because it looked like something she should know, and now, on Thursday, Ms. Yang was asking her to stand up and defend it.

The room smelled like old carpet and the librarian's coffee. Six of them had signed up for the free coding week, and the final project required a search function for a sorted list of two thousand book titles, actual titles from the library's catalog. Ms. Yang had them split into two teams. Sawyer's team was nearly done with a loop that checked every title from the first one onward. Peyton's team had nothing, because Peyton had spent two days arguing with Annabella about approach instead of writing code.

"Peyton," Ms. Yang said, tapping the whiteboard with the cap of her marker. "You wrote this. The group votes in twenty minutes on which search we use. Convince us, or tell us you can't."

Peyton's face went hot. She hadn't written it. She had copied it, which was not the same thing, and she opened her mouth to say so, then closed it. The distinction felt thin. She was the one who had put it on paper, put it forward, and if it was wrong, the culpability sat with her regardless of whose hand had held the original marker. Annabella was watching her with the flat patience of someone who had already written a for-loop in her head.

"I can show you," Peyton said, "instead of telling you." She went to the shelf of dictionaries Ms. Yang kept at the back, the glacial pace of her walk deliberate, buying seconds. She carried the thickest one back and set it on the table.

"Linear search is how Sawyer's team does it," she said. "You start at page one and check every word until you find the one you want." She flipped the dictionary open to A. "Programmers call it O(n), which means the work grows in step with the list. Two thousand titles, you might check two thousand titles."

Sawyer leaned back. "So what's yours, magic?"

Peyton opened the dictionary to the exact middle. "I look here. One word, one check. The word I want is either on this page, before it, or after it. If it's after, I tear off everything before this page in my head." She turned to the middle of the remaining half. "Again. One check, half the book gone." She kept halving, out loud, walking her fingers through the pages, and Sawyer, despite himself, leaned in to see where she'd land.

"That's maybe fifteen checks," he said slowly, "for the whole dictionary."

"For the whole dictionary." She hadn't known that number an hour ago. She had found it last night in a library book on algorithms, sitting alone at a carrel after the fight with Annabella, still stinging from it. The book had said the phrase on her notebook meant something specific: binary search was O(log n), meaning its work grew with the logarithm of the list's size, not in step with the list itself. She had read the sentence four times. The word logarithm had sat there like a locked door. She understood the halving, though. She understood the dictionary. She was not entirely sure she understood how the one became the other, and she did not pretend to, even to herself.

"There's a catch," she said. "It only works if the list is sorted. If the titles aren't in order, halving tells you nothing. That's why nobody uses it on messy data."

Ms. Yang wrote vote on the whiteboard and underlined it. "Twenty minutes starts now. Teams, decide."

Sawyer began to remonstrate, saying they'd already built half the loop, that starting over at the eleventh hour was reckless, that Peyton's team didn't even have working code. Annabella cut him off, which surprised Peyton more than anything else that afternoon. "Write the fifteen lines," Annabella said to Peyton, quietly, sliding the laptop across the table. "I'll sort the titles. You showed it works. Now prove it."

Peyton's hands hovered over the keyboard. She knew the shape of the thing, the low index and the high index and the middle between them, but she had never typed it live with five people watching. The vote was in eighteen minutes. She set low to zero, high to 1999, and found the middle.

"Fingers crossed," she said, and hit run.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
Hannah spread the newspaper across her grandmother's kitchen table, the one with the oilcloth gone soft at the corners, and smoothed the crease with the heel of her hand. The article was four paragraphs in German, assigned by Ms. Becker for Monday: read it, then summarise it aloud without notes. Her grandmother had offered the kitchen, the good light, and a plate of plum cake as if these were reasonable substitutes for fluency.

"Langsam," her grandmother said, lowering herself into the opposite chair with the sound old knees make. "Read it slowly. Not like your grandfather, who swallowed the newspaper whole and told you only the parts that upset him."

Hannah began at the first full sentence, which was about flood damage, and worked her way down, dictionary open beside the cake. Somewhere in the second paragraph she realised she had been skipping over the small cluster of words at the top of the article, the ones in capitals before the first sentence began. She had taken them for a headline fragment, or some decoration of layout, and she had been doing the same thing all week with the practice articles Ms. Becker had posted. She traced her finger back up to them. WIEN, they said. Vienna. The story she had carefully decoded was not about the town described in its paragraphs at all, or rather it was, but the reporting had come from somewhere else entirely, and she had never once asked where.

She thought of Zane, then, with a small cold drop in her stomach. On Thursday he had summarised his article and told the class the story came from Switzerland, and Ms. Becker had asked him to look again at the very top of the page, and he had gone red and said, "Oh. The dateline. I skipped the dateline." The word had slid past her at the time. Now it didn't. The dateline named the city where the story was reported, and it sat there before the first sentence, quietly doing its work while readers like Hannah and Zane ploughed straight into the verbs.

"Do you know what this is," she asked, tapping the capitals, "this word before the sentence?"

Her grandmother pulled the paper closer, and Hannah watched something shift in her face, a door opening onto a room she hadn't visited in a while. "Natürlich. We had a newspaper every day when I was young. You always looked there first. It told you how far away the news was, whether it had travelled all night to reach you."

That was the first real thing Hannah had learned all afternoon, and it had nothing to do with the flood. "Say that again about the travelling," she said, but her grandmother had already turned toward the window, where the garden was going brown at the edges, and said, "Your grandfather delivered papers. That is how he got his legs, all that bicycle. He would say he married me for my father's subscription."

They worked through the rest of the article together, Hannah reading aloud, halting, correcting, her grandmother supplying words the dictionary gave too many options for. Twice Hannah caught herself about to prevaricate when her grandmother asked whether she understood a clause, mumbling "more or less," and both times the old woman just waited, patient as weather, until Hannah went back and actually parsed it. There was no duress in it, no clock ticking, and that was what made it bearable: school German was all performance under time, and this was something slower and more honest, though it cost her something too. She could feel her afternoon draining away, the messages from Sarah-Eve accumulating unanswered in her pocket, the last Friday of the summer shortening outside the window while she sat inside conjugating.

When she finally stood and summarised the article aloud, in German, twice, she made herself start with the city. "In Wien," she began, and heard her own voice steady on it. She left things out. She knew she left things out, whole threads about aid money and a minister whose title she couldn't render, and she decided not to pretend otherwise. "I have the flood and the cost and the town," she said, switching to English, "and I am guessing it is critical of the government, but I am not sure how much of that is in the words and how much is me wanting it there."

"Then say you are not sure," her grandmother said, cutting her a second slice of cake she hadn't asked for. "A summary that knows its own edges is worth more than a big one full of holes."

Hannah wasn't certain that was true, or true everywhere; Ms. Becker gave marks, and marks did not always reward honesty about limits. She took the slice anyway. Her phone buzzed again against her hip and she left it where it was, face down on the oilcloth, while she copied the dateline word for word into her notebook and underlined it twice.

On Monday Zane went first again, and this time he began, "In Berlin," without being asked. When Hannah's turn came, she opened her mouth and found she was nervous in a way she hadn't been at the kitchen table, the classroom clock ticking on the wall above Ms. Becker's head. "In Wien," she said.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
Austin had a clipboard, which he felt was half the job. The other half was seven twelve-year-olds who could not pass, and the clipboard was not helping with them. He stood at the elbow of the outdoor court behind the middle school, whistle borrowed from his own coach looped around his neck, and watched a chest pass sail over everyone's head and into the chain-link fence.

Mr. Papadopoulos, who ran the rec league, had handed him the team three weeks ago with the words "Fix the passing and you've fixed the team," which Austin had taken as a mission rather than an offhand remark. He'd drawn up drills, three of them, each targeting a specific flaw: the bounce pass that died halfway, the skip pass thrown into double coverage, the panic pass made with eyes closed. He ran the drills and he coached them the only way he knew how, which was the way his father had coached him. Every pass got a verdict. "Elbows in." "Look first." "Too soft." "Too hard." He liked the sound of his own corrections; they made him feel like he knew something.

Nancy came to watch on Thursdays, mostly, she claimed, to do homework somewhere with better weather than her kitchen. She sat on the low wall with a chemistry binder and watched him call out two hundred judgments in an hour. "You talk more than the games do," she said.

The proof came at the Saturday scrimmage. Austin had to stay quiet, since it was a game and he'd read that coaches who shout through games teach kids to listen instead of play, though maybe he'd made that up. Either way he kept his mouth shut, and his team fell apart. Passes went to nobody. Marcus, his best passer in drills, stood with the ball at the top of the key turning in slow circles like a man waiting for directions that were not coming. They lost by eighteen, and the worst part was that the passing drills had looked beautiful all week. Something he had built worked only while he was standing there holding it up.

He found the answer at one in the morning, in his mother's old college textbook, opened for no reason he could later defend. It was a paragraph about motor learning, and there was a name in it, and the name was the thing he recognized himself in. At practice on Monday he pulled Nancy aside before the kids arrived.

"It's called the guidance hypothesis," he said. "Feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it. Less frequent feedback helps retention." He read it off his phone because he was afraid of getting it wrong in the air.

"So you're the problem," Nancy said. "Congratulations."

"I'm the problem," Austin said. He had been thinking of his father's coaching as a kind of inheritance, something a man inculcates in a boy by repetition until it becomes instinct. Now he was undergoing a small revisionist moment about his whole childhood: maybe the constant corrections hadn't made him better. Maybe they'd made him need them. He could not decide this, and he was honest with himself about not being able to, because he'd also hit some very good shots in his life and somebody had to have said "elbows in" first.

The new rule: corrections only after every fifth pass, or after a full drill, never one at a time. The kids noticed immediately, in the way kids notice a change in weather. "You're not yelling," Marcus said, sounding cheated.

"I'm being sagacious," Austin said. He did not fully know what the word meant, but he'd looked it up that morning and it seemed safe, and Marcus laughed anyway, and then, on the next rep, threw a bounce pass that actually arrived at a teammate's hands, and Austin said nothing, and the silence felt like it cost him money.

The following Saturday they lost by six. Then they won by four, and the winning pass was a skip pass, thrown by Marcus before the double team arrived, to a kid in the corner nobody had been open for a second earlier. Austin kept his hands in his pockets the whole possession. Afterward Marcus ran over, jubilant, and demanded to know what Austin had seen from the sideline, what the great coaching insight had been. Austin considered telling him the truth, which was that the insight had been to shut up, and that he still wasn't sure whether it worked or whether the kids had simply grown, that he could not yet separate his silence from their improvement and might never be able to.

"That pass was all you," Austin said. "Do it again next week and I'll say something nice about it eventually."

"Eventually," Marcus repeated, and jogged back to the huddle, ball under one arm, already calling for it.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
Katherine's grandmother had given her exactly one piece of driving advice, delivered over Thanksgiving pie with the gravity of a state secret: if you ever have to stop fast, pump the brakes. Pump them, Katie, or you'll lock up and go wherever the car decides. Katherine had nodded and filed it away next to the grandmother's other certainties, which included never banking on Fridays and always carrying exact change.

Now it was Saturday morning, and the family car was idling in the church parking lot with Ms. Pierre in the passenger seat. Ms. Pierre was a retired driving examiner who lived three houses down and agreed to teach Katherine because, she said, she trusted the family's brakes more than she trusted the driving school's. She had a clipboard she never wrote on and a thermos she sipped from at stop signs, which Katherine found both reassuring and slightly theatrical.

"Hands at nine and three," Ms. Pierre said. "Not ten and two, that's the old way. Everything about driving has an old way." She set down the thermos. "Let's do some braking. Drive to the far end and stop at that light pole. Stop as if a child ran out, not as if the pole did."
