Katherine drove the length of the lot and braked hard. The car lurched and stopped short of the pole, and she sat gripping the wheel, pleased with herself.

"Now do it again, but this time I'm going to tell you mid-brake to swerve left. That's how emergencies actually happen, in pieces."

They looped around and tried again. Halfway through the stop, Ms. Pierre said "Now, left," and Katherine pumped the brakes, just as her grandmother had instructed, and turned the wheel, and the car slid a lazy, wide arc that ended well past the pole, pointed at a hedge. Ms. Pierre put one hand on the dashboard and made a sound Katherine chose to interpret as philosophical.

"Where did you learn to pump?" Ms. Pierre asked.

"My grandmother. She said you lock up otherwise."

Ms. Pierre looked out at the hedge for a moment, the way she looked at things she was deciding not to argue with yet. "What year is this car?"

"2019."

"Take us around again. Brake hard and hold the pedal down, all the way, and steer while you do it. Trust the pedal. It'll feel strange, like it's arguing with you. Keep holding."

Katherine circled back, accelerated to the speed Ms. Pierre indicated, and braked with everything she had. The pedal shuddered under her foot, a fast mechanical chatter, and her instinct was to let go, because a pedal that fights you must be winning. She held it and turned the wheel, and the car slowed and turned together, neatly, stopping just left of the pole in a length of lot she would have sworn was too short.

"The pedal's supposed to do that," Ms. Pierre said. "You kept your foot in it and you kept steering. That's the whole skill."

"So when Gran said pump," Katherine said slowly, working through it, "that was true for her old car. In this one, I press hard and hold it, and I can still steer." She said it out loud partly for herself, because saying it made it hers, and partly because she was already composing how she'd say it again over pie at Christmas.

"Old advice, old brakes," Ms. Pierre said. "Your grandmother wasn't wrong for her car. She's just still driving that car in her head." She picked up her thermos, nonchalant, as if a sixteen-year-old had not just nearly fertilized a hedge with a Camry.

Katherine thought about that on the drive home, Ms. Pierre having surrendered the lesson's last ten minutes to "residential roads, keep it boring." The probity of the situation, as Ms. Pierre would probably put it, since she used words like that, was that both her grandmother and the pedal had told the truth. The grandmother's truth was just twenty years stale. Katherine wasn't sure which unsettled her more: that adults could be confidently out of date, or that the car itself, a machine, was quietly more current than all of them. She decided she could hold both of those at once without resolving them, which felt like something she'd be doing a lot of in the next few years.

That evening her father asked how it went, and she said fine, and that the parking lot had a hedge she now respected. He laughed and asked what else. She started to explain the brakes, saw his eyes drift toward his phone on the counter, and stopped.

At Thanksgiving she sat beside her grandmother with a second piece of pie and waited for the question she knew was coming, because the family's attention had a way of circling back to whoever had recently been behind a wheel. Her grandmother set down her fork.

"So. Driving. What did they teach you first?"

Katherine took a breath. "You know that car of ours has anti-lock brakes, Gran? Press firm and hold, and you can still steer the whole time. No pumping."

Her grandmother looked at her for a long moment, then out the window at the driveway, where the Camry sat gleaming and silent and, Katherine thought, a little smug.

"Well," her grandmother said, and reached for her coffee.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Near Earth's surface a projectile's vertical velocity changes by about 9.8 metres per second every second, whether it is rising or falling.
story:
The worksheet had seventeen problems on it and Owen had finished none of them, which he considered a kind of consistency. Problem four showed a ball launched at an angle with a little arrow for velocity, and beside it the instruction: resolve into components. He read that as an accusation. The room was the physics lab after last period, three desks still occupied, and Ms. Hoffmann was at her desk grading with a red pen she seemed to ration, like a penurious landlord deciding which repairs the building truly needed.

"You're staring at it like it owes you money," Dean said from the next desk.

"It owes me an answer."

Elie, two rows up, turned around. She had finished six problems and was doing a seventh for entertainment, which Owen found abrasive. "You're treating the velocity as one thing," she said. "It's two things happening at once."

"That sounds like a circumlocution for 'I don't know.'"

"It's arithmetic. Sideways and up-and-down don't talk to each other. The sideways part just keeps going. Only the vertical part changes."

Owen looked at the arrow on his page. It pointed up and to the right, confident in a way he resented, and he was expected to split it into a horizontal piece and a vertical piece and track each one separately through the air, as if the ball were two balls occupying the same space, one traveling placidly forward forever and the other living a much more dramatic life.

At home that evening he decided the only honest test was a ball. He found a stopwatch app on his phone, stood in the driveway, and threw a tennis ball almost straight up, timing it. It rose, hung at the top like it was considering its options, and came down. His first throw gave him 2.4 seconds total. He threw again: 2.6. He threw a third time and his younger brother appeared at the window to watch, which Owen chose not to interpret.

He sat on the front step and did what the worksheet refused to do for him, which was think. The ball took half the time going up and half coming down. So if the whole flight was 2.6 seconds, the fall was 1.3 seconds. He knew one number from class, written on the board and underlined twice: near the ground, vertical velocity changes by about 9.8 metres per second every second. That was the rate, the same rate, all the way through. He tested it against the throw. If the ball gained 9.8 metres per second of speed during each second of the fall, then after 1.3 seconds it was falling at nearly 13 metres per second. Which meant it had been thrown upward at nearly 13 metres per second too, because the trip up and the trip down matched. The ball slowed on the way up at exactly the same rate it sped up coming down, whether rising or falling, like a rule with no exceptions printed on it anywhere.

This surprised him more than he admitted to the driveway. He had assumed, without ever saying so to himself, that going up was one story and coming down was another. That a thing fought harder against you than it cooperated. He threw the ball again, watching it more than timing it, and it did look like the same event played forward and then in reverse, which felt like a trick he'd been failing to notice his entire life.

The next day he finished eleven of the seventeen problems in the lab after school. On problem nine he made an error, using half the total time for the horizontal distance instead of the whole time, and Elie circled it without speaking, which was more instructive than any speech would have been. He fixed it. The sideways velocity never changed, so the horizontal distance was just that steady speed times the whole flight, and the vertical part did its rising-and-falling arithmetic underneath, and the two halves of the ball reunited at the answer.

"Better," Ms. Hoffmann said, passing his desk. She put a small check beside problem four, and he felt absurdly absolved, forgiven for a sin no one had named.

"I still don't get why it's the same rate going up and coming down," Owen said.

"Nobody asked you to get why," she said, and moved on to the next desk.

Owen looked at his page, at the arrow now broken into a quiet horizontal line and a vertical one, and decided the why could wait for college. He picked up the pen and started problem ten.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: If air resistance is ignored, a projectile's horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight, because no horizontal force acts on it.
story:
The makeup test was Monday morning, and Hailey had spent Saturday afternoon at the kitchen table failing to care about it, so on Sunday she put the worksheet in her backpack and rode her bike to the skate park off Delmore Road with the idea that she would watch Kaelan instead of studying. Mr. Chowdhury had written one comment at the top of her failed quiz: "Separate the components. Try watching something fall." She assumed he meant it as a joke, since he knew she spent Sundays here.

The park emptied out in stages. The diurnal crowd, small kids and their parents, cleared off around five, and then the older skaters claimed the bowls in the long orange light. Hailey sat on the low wall near the quarter pipe with the worksheet on her knee and her phone in her hand. Kaelan was dropping in off the ledge on the far side, the one that hung maybe a metre and a half above the flat, and Meganne was filming him on her own phone, crouched low to catch the flight.

"You're supposed to be studying," Meganne said, without lowering the phone.

"I am studying." Hailey held up the worksheet. Problem four showed a ball launched horizontally off a table at four metres per second and asked how far it landed from the base. She had gotten it wrong twice by trying to average the speed somehow, as though the ball remembered being slower or faster than it was.

Kaelan rolled up next to the wall, breathing hard. "Film me off the ledge," he said. "The whole flight, not cut off at the end like last time."

"Get the landing in or it's useless," Hailey said, and moved along the wall so she could see the launch point and the flat ground beyond it. She asked Kaelan to roll a marker along the flat, a slow push so she could time it, and he did, puzzled but willing. Ten metres in 5.9 seconds, she worked out on the back of the worksheet. His rolling speed along the ground was about 1.7 metres per second. Then she filmed the whole flight off the ledge, launch to landing, and stepped the video frame by frame.

"Sixty frames," she said. "That's two seconds." The ledge was one and a half metres high. She didn't need the height yet; what she needed was the distance, so she paced from the wall to the scuff mark where his board had first touched concrete, heel to toe, eight times plus a bit. Roughly six metres. And the launch speed along the top of the ledge was the same rolling speed she had measured on the flat, because he wasn't pushing off, only rolling off, nothing added.

"Six metres in two seconds is three metres per second," she said. "That's not your rolling speed."

Kaelan came and looked at her numbers, dripping sweat onto the paper. "You measured wrong."

"I measured twice." She had. The distance was six metres and the time was two seconds, and the speed at the top was 1.7. Somewhere in the flight he had gained horizontal speed, which made no sense to her until she looked at the frames again and saw what he was actually doing in the air, leaning back, kicking the board forward underneath him, dragging it ahead of his body.

"You're pulling it," she said. "In the air. You speed it up yourself." He took the phone and stepped through the frames and admitted it, sheepish, because it was a habit he'd built from the genealogy of ledge tricks everyone at this park learned from everyone older, a kick passed down through skaters neither of them had ever met, and it was invisible to him until the frames isolated it.

"Then do it without the kick," she said. "Just roll off dead."

He did it three times, and Meganne filmed all three, complaining about the light going. Without the kick the numbers closed: 1.7 metres per second horizontally, flight time two seconds, landing spot three and a half metres out from the wall, matching every time. She wrote it on the worksheet in the margin of problem four. If you ignored air resistance, the horizontal velocity stayed constant for the whole flight, because no horizontal force acted on it. Nothing pushed it sideways, so nothing about the sideways motion changed, from the instant it left the ledge to the instant it landed. Only the vertical part kept changing. She separated them on paper the way the frames had separated them in the air, and did problem four in four lines: three seconds of falling, twelve metres from the base.

The ball didn't slow down going out and it didn't speed up, not on its own, and Kaelan's board had only seemed to because Kaelan himself was the extra force. That was the part she still turned over as the light went grey and the first lamps buzzed on. She recalibrated her estimate of how much of what looked like physics in the world was actually somebody's habit, and how much of her own quiz answers had been that same kind of invisible self-interference, errors she couldn't see without the frame-by-frame. Meganne packed up the phone. Kaelan rolled back toward the ledge for one more before full dark.

"Say the line again," he called over his shoulder, pushing off. "The thing about the horizontal."

Hailey stood on the wall with the worksheet flapping in her hand and shouted it after him: "Constant the whole flight, if you ignore air resistance, because nothing's acting on it sideways!"

He dropped in without the kick, and she started the timer.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
The laminated sheet taped to the pool office door had six lines on it, and Angelina read them twice before practice on Tuesday. Step one was rest, complete rest, no screens, no practice, nothing. After that came light activity, then sport-specific work without risk of contact, then drills with contact, then full practice, and finally a meet. Beside each line, in Mr. Yamamoto's small blocky handwriting, was a note: only move up when free of symptoms. She had been on step one for nine days.

"You're counting again," Daniyal said, dropping his bag on the bench beside hers. He was the only other person there at six forty, the two of them always early because the late bus was unreliable.

"Nine days of nothing. I watched the ceiling."

"Better than the alternative."

She didn't ask which alternative he meant. The headache had gone on day seven, and yesterday Mr. Yamamoto had cleared her for step two, which meant the stationary bike in the equipment room for twenty minutes, no pool. Today, if the bike went fine, she could try light activity in the water. Kicking with a board, easy laps, nothing fast.

The pool was quiet at that hour, the water flat and pale green under the deck lights. Mr. Yamamoto stood at the shallow end with a clipboard and a stopwatch he wasn't using. "Board, kick, easy," he said. "If anything comes back, you get out. Anything."

She pushed off the wall. The water was colder than she remembered, or her body had forgotten how to read it. Fifty meters of kicking felt like nothing, a warm-up she had done a thousand times, and she turned at the far wall feeling almost ordinary. On the second length she noticed a pressure behind her right eye, small, like a thumb pressing gently. She told herself it was the chlorine. On the third length the thumb pressed harder.

She stopped at the wall and put the board on the deck. "It's back," she said. "A little. Behind my eye."

Mr. Yamamoto crouched, forearms on his knees. "Then you're done for today."

"I did two lengths fine."

"You step back," he said. "That's how it works."

"I'm not back to step one," she said, and heard how peevish it came out, and didn't take it back.

"Back a stage. Rest again until it clears."

She sat on the edge with her fins in her lap and watched Daniyal swim his warm-up, clean and unhurried, flip turns stacking up behind him like punctuation. She had been going to ascribe the headache to the cold water, or to not eating enough, or to sleeping badly on Sunday, because any of those could be fixed. A body that couldn't tolerate three easy lengths was a different problem. It had a protocol and a clipboard and a man with a stopwatch deciding when she was allowed to be an athlete again.

Cailyn arrived late, hair still damp from a shower at home, and sat beside her on the bench. "How's the head?"

"I got three lengths in and it came back. Now I'm back to rest."

"That happened to me in the fall. I tried to skip through it." Cailyn pulled her cap on. "I ended up missing the whole season instead of three weeks. Coach called my two-week self a travesty of patience."

Angelina laughed, one syllable, mostly air. "I don't want to be patient. The conference meet is in five weeks."

"So be bored instead. Bored is fine. Bored is rest."

Cailyn dropped into the water and joined Daniyal's lane, and the two of them settled into a rhythm Angelina knew without swimming, the splash and turn, the counting of lengths. Mr. Yamamoto came over and stood beside her, clipboard against his hip. He didn't say anything reassuring, which she decided she preferred. The sheet on the office door had never promised she would get through all six steps in order, only that each one had to be earned. What she couldn't know was how many days rest would take this time, and whether the steps ahead of her were a ladder or a staircase she would keep falling down. She looked at the water, green and evenly lit, and at the clock above the far wall.

"Can I time them?" she said. "Just to have something to do."

He handed her the stopwatch.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: By the JavaBeans naming convention, a getter for a field named 'score' is called getScore(), and a getter for a boolean field is usually named with 'is', like isActive().
story:
The library's third floor smelled of carpet cleaner and old toner, and the radiator by the window ticked like a slow clock. Jade spread Drayden's printout across two tables: forty pages of a class file he had written at midnight, apparently, without once checking it. Their project was due Thursday. Their test class ran to ninety errors.

"Look at this one," Gregoire said, tapping a line. "fetchScore." He turned a page. "And here it's grabScore. And here, just score."

Drayden slumped into the chair across from them, hood up. "It's my code. I'll name them what I want."

"Then nobody can read it," Jade said. "Not even you. Look, page twelve. You called the same thing two different names."

He pulled the hood lower and said nothing, which Jade had learned meant he knew she was right and would rather be swallowed by the floor than accede out loud. She let it sit. The radiator ticked. Somewhere below them a printer ground through a job with the throughput of melting honey, sheet by reluctant sheet.

She opened the textbook she'd carried up, the one Ms. Côté had left on the reserve shelf with a sticky note reading "for the group who keeps fighting." Ms. Côté never said things directly. The chapter on encapsulation had a paragraph on private fields, and Jade read it twice, then turned to the section on naming. There it was, plain as a bus schedule. She read it aloud before she could edit herself. "A getter for a field named score is called getScore." She looked up. "That's the convention. JavaBeans."

Drayden's hood shifted. "What?"

"getScore," Jade said again, slower. "And for a boolean it's usually is. Like isActive."

Gregoire was already flipping through Drayden's pages, and the tally came out worse than any of them expected. fetchScore, grabScore, retrieveScore, and once, magnificently, procureScore. For the boolean field active, Drayden had written checkActive, isActive, and activeStatus, three getters for one field, two of which did not exist where the test class called them. That was a third of the ninety errors right there.

"So it's not just style," Gregoire said. "The test calls the names it expects. We fail the tests because of the names."

Drayden pulled his laptop over without a word. For a while there was only typing, the click of Jade's pen against the table, and the turbid light coming through the frosted windows, the sun gone the color of weak tea behind the glass. He renamed one getter, then another. At procureScore he paused.

"That one's staying," he said.

"You're joking," Jade said.

"It's the best word in the file." But his mouth twitched, and then his hands were moving again, and procureScore became getScore, and the printout went into the recycling bin page by page, forty pages, folded once each.

By the time the library announcement came over the ceiling speakers, the test class had gone from ninety errors to eleven, and then to three, and then Drayden pressed run again and the output pane filled with green. Jade leaned back so far her chair creaked. She understood now what Ms. Côté's sticky note had actually been doing, which was not fixing them but handing them a rule they could fight about instead of fighting about each other. Whether a convention was a cage or a kindness she still couldn't say, and she said so, and Gregoire shrugged, and Drayden said the convention was fine, whatever, which from him was a speech.

They packed up in the dark, jackets and cables and the sticky note, which Jade pocketed for reasons she didn't examine. On the stairs her phone buzzed: Ms. Côté, to the whole group.

"Small change," the message read. "I've swapped partners for the final unit. Drayden, you're with me."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
The licensing office smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Mason stood in line holding a numbered ticket like it might disintegrate. His father had driven him here and then sat in the car outside, because his father's presence in any government building lately made him sweat. The print shop's solvency was a word Mason had overheard through the wall of his bedroom for three months now, spoken into phones at midnight, and the driving lesson was a small luxury his father had insisted on anyway, as if competence could be bought in installments, like anything else.

Mason was third in line when Klara appeared beside him, backpack over one shoulder, sunglasses pushed up into her hair. She had gotten her license in March and had been unbearable about it in a way that was mostly affectionate. Vivian trailed behind her with two iced coffees and a quizlet she was failing to ignore, her thumb flicking through vocabulary words for the English final.

"Autochthonous," Vivian read aloud. "Means originating in the place where it's found. Native."

"That's you," Klara said to Mason. "Born in this line, will die in this line."

The window opened, the clerk scanned his permit, stamped something, and directed him to the far doors where the driving school's cars were parked in a neat diagonal row. Each car was white with a rooftop sign, and each sign, Mason noticed, was underwritten by an insurance company whose logo he recognized from late-night commercials. That was the arrangement, apparently: the state licensed you, the school taught you, and somewhere a company assumed the risk of your incompetence at a calculated price.

His instructor was Ms. Chea, a small woman in her sixties with reading glasses on a chain and an unhurried voice. She had him adjust the seat, the wheel, the mirrors, and then walk once around the car, touching each tire, because, she said, a driver should know what the car looks like before the car knows anything about you. Mason did it, feeling Klara and Vivian watching from the curb, Vivian mouthing autochthonous at him like a curse.

The first twenty minutes were tame. A parking lot, then quiet residential streets where he signaled too early and braked too gently, and Ms. Chea said "good" in the tone of someone grading on a curve. Then she directed him onto a four-lane road and told him, at the next light, to move into the left lane. The light changed. Mason signaled, checked the mirror, checked it again, and began to turn the wheel.

"Stop." Ms. Chea's hand was on the wheel, firm, not panicked. A silver hatchback slid past on his left, close enough that he heard the hum of its tires, close enough that his stomach dropped through the floor of the car. "That's your blind spot," she said. "Can't see it from the seat, even with the mirrors. That's why you turn your head."

He pulled over where she told him to and sat with his hands at ten and two, gripping. The hatchback's driver, a man in a work vest, glanced over as he passed, and Mason expected anger and got instead a small nod, the acknowledgment of one person who remembered being that person. In the mirror, Klara and Vivian had stood up from the curb.

"The mirrors lie?" Mason asked.

"The mirrors show what they show," Ms. Chea said. "Everything else, you have to look for."

They practiced it. Turn signal, mirror, and then the head check, a quick turn of the chin toward the window, and the first few times Mason's hands drifted the wheel the way his head went, which Ms. Chea corrected with two words, hands steady, until the two motions separated and became independent, one part of him looking and another part holding the line. On the fourth attempt he caught a delivery van sitting exactly where the hatchback had been, invisible in the glass and plain as day through the window, and he waited, and it passed, and he moved left with a whole lane of empty road around him.

Afterward, at the curb, Klara asked how it went, and Mason found he could not summarize it honestly. He told them about the hatchback and watched Vivian wince. He had walked into the licensing office believing that careful was the same as safe, that if he checked the mirror twice the world owed him a true report, and now he knew there were places a person could not see from where he sat, that being careful meant turning his whole head and accepting that even then something could be there. Whether the lesson would hold, whether his hands would stay steady the first time his father let him take the car out alone, he honestly did not know. His father was leaning against the car across the lot, arms folded, waiting.

"Autochthonous," Vivian said, offering him the last of her coffee. "Native to the place where it's found."

"I'm going to be native to the passenger seat for a while," Mason said, and Ms. Chea, signing his lesson card through the window, told him to be there Saturday at nine.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime.
story:
The moving truck idled in front of the new house while her father counted boxes aloud, as if numbering them might make them fewer. "You know," he said, closing the truck's rear door, "a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime. That's Census data, 2007 survey." Brooklyn didn't look up from her phone, where Stella's last message sat unanswered: you're going to be fine, you always are. She typed nothing back. Eleven point seven moves, and this was only her second, and already the number felt less like a statistic than a sentence.

She started school on a Tuesday, mid-September, when everyone else had already learned each other's names and shortcuts through the hallways. Mr. Njoroge, who taught her economics elective, gave her a seat near the window and a packet of work she'd have to catch up on alone. At lunch she found a table of girls laughing about something that had happened in August, before she existed here, and she took the empty seat at the end and opened her sandwich like it was paperwork.

A girl named Kathy sat down across from her on the third day. "You're in my econ class," Kathy said. "Njoroge gives the hardest unit test first, on purpose, to scare people into dropping. Nobody drops." Brooklyn said she wasn't planning to. Kathy nodded, apparently satisfied, and started describing the town with the flat affection of someone who had never considered leaving it: the good pizza place, the bad pizza place, the creek that flooded every spring.

The test was on a Friday. Brooklyn had spent the week studying at the kitchen table between unpacked boxes marked KITCHEN and MORE KITCHEN, texting Stella photos of her textbook pages so Stella could quiz her from three hundred miles away. It worked, mostly. Stella's questions arrived with jokes attached, little burnished reminders of a language only the two of them spoke, and for the length of a quiz session Brooklyn could pretend the distance was a technicality. But at the test, Mr. Njoroge put a question on the board about opportunity cost that Stella hadn't covered, and Brooklyn sat with her pen still for four full minutes before she wrote anything.

She got a 91. Mr. Njoroge handed the papers back and said, "You catch up fast," which was the first thing anyone at the school had said about her that wasn't a question. Walking out, she checked her phone. Stella had sent a photo of the parking spot where they used to eat lunch, captioned RIP. Brooklyn understood it was meant as affection, but standing in a hallway full of strangers, it landed like a small bill she was expected to pay, some recompense for having left without dying.

That weekend her father found her crying over a box of old yearbooks and did the worst thing, which was to be kind. "You'll make friends," he said. "You already have, that Kathy seems nice." Brooklyn said it wasn't the same, and he said nothing, and his silence was more honest than reassurance would have been. Later she did the arithmetic herself: 11.7 moves in a lifetime, and if this was her second at eighteen, the rest were out there waiting, and she could either treat each one as a loss to be mourned or as a thing that simply happened to people, like weather.

On Monday, Kathy asked if she wanted to see the creek that flooded every spring. It was dry that day, a concrete channel with a shopping cart lodged in it, and Kathy talked the whole walk there about a boy in her chemistry class with an insouciant way of never doing homework and somehow passing. Brooklyn laughed at the right places. Then she took out her phone and, standing on the creek's dry bed, typed to Stella: met a girl who talks like kathy from the bus, you'd like her. It wasn't exactly true. She wasn't sure yet whether she liked Kathy or was merely grateful to her, and she wasn't sure whether staying in touch with Stella would hold the friendship together or slowly prove it couldn't survive without the parking spot, without the shared Augusts.

But she sent it anyway, and put the phone in her pocket, and followed Kathy up the bank toward the road.

"Tomorrow," Kathy called over her shoulder, "I'm showing you the bad pizza place."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In the United States, courts generally will not enforce a liability waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it.
story:
The clipper jammed twice before it cut the wristband, and Elliot swept the plastic curls into his palm while the customer was still signing the digital pad at the front desk. He had worked at Summit Vertical for six weeks, long enough to know that nobody read what they signed. They scrawled, they initialed, they tapped the green button that said I AGREE, and then they asked where the bathroom was.

It was a Friday evening in October, and the gym smelled of chalk and rubber. Behind him the auto-belay lanes clanked their slow mechanical rhythm. He was supposed to check the waiver queue, restock the chalk bins, and explain the rental shoe sizes with the patience of a saint, which he mostly managed. The trouble had started on Tuesday, when a man had fallen from the top of the bouldering wall, landed wrong on the pad, and been carried out with his ankle wrapped in a compression bandage. The man had signed the waiver. Everyone signed the waiver. Elliot had signed it himself before he was hired, skimming the dense paragraphs of capitalized text, and now he could not stop wondering what he had actually agreed to.

"Elliot, wall four," called Rami from across the floor. Rami had been there a year and treated every shift like a surf movie. "Climber wants a reroute on the 5.9."

"After I clear the queue." A woman at the desk was squinting at the tablet, her thumb hovering. "What does this mean, assumption of risk?" she asked.

"It means climbing is dangerous and you know it," Elliot said, and hated how rehearsed it sounded, like the phrasing had been cauterized into him during training, sealed off from question.

"Do I have any rights at all if something happens?"

He opened his mouth and realized he did not know. He told her the manager could help, and took her question into the back office like a stone in his shoe.

Mr. Ba was reviewing inventory, a clipboard in one hand. He had run the gym for eleven years and had the calm of a man who had watched many people fall and get up again. Elliot asked him straight out: what is the gym actually still responsible for?

Mr. Ba set the clipboard down. "What do you think?"

"I think a signed piece of paper can't cover everything. But I don't know where the line is."

"Good. Find out, then tell me." He said it without irony, the way he said most things, and turned back to the crates of carabiners.

Elliot spent his break in the stairwell with his phone, the signal flickering. He read forum threads, then a page that looked official, then more forum threads. What he found gave him a strange, cold relief. Courts would not enforce a waiver that tried to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person had signed it. He read the sentence three times. Ordinary negligence was what you signed away, the ordinary risks of an ordinary gym. But if someone had done something truly reckless, or worse, meant harm, the signature meant nothing. A waiver was not an absolution. It was a boundary, and boundaries implied a beyond.

Tyrone came down the stairs with a broom and found him sitting on the third step. "You look like you saw a ghost."

"Sort of the opposite." Elliot showed him the screen. Tyrone read slowly, lips moving, which Elliot had learned not to comment on.

"So the waiver's partly fake?"

"It's real for the stuff it's real for. It's fake for the stuff it can't be real for."

Tyrone considered this the way he considered most things, with his whole face. "Then why do we make everyone sign it?"

"Because most falls are just falls."

When his break ended, Elliot went back to the desk and did something he had never done. When the next customer, a college kid in a denim jacket, slid the tablet toward the signature line, Elliot said, "You don't have to sign it fast. Most people don't read it. I didn't, the first time."

The kid looked up. "Is it bad?"

"It says you accept the normal risks. It can't excuse everything, no matter what it says." He kept it short, the way a fact should be, and slid the tablet back so the kid could actually look.

The kid read for a whole minute while the line behind him grew and Rami made urgent gestures from the shoe wall. Somewhere above them a climber slapped the sedimentary ridges of the artificial wall, chalk puffing off her hands, and the auto-belays clanked on, indifferent as tide. The kid signed, but he read it first, and handed the tablet back with a small nod, like something had been settled between them.

Elliot turned to the next customer. "First time climbing?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
The church smelled of lilies and floor wax, and the pews were fuller than Payton had expected, which made the waiting worse. Her grandfather's coffin sat at the front beneath a spray of white flowers, and the organist played something interminable while latecomers filed in. Payton kept her eyes on the coffin's brass handles because looking at her mother's back, rigid and small in the first pew, made her chest do something she couldn't afford yet. She had a reading to do, the twenty-third psalm, printed on a folded card her aunt had handed her that morning, and she had practiced until the words held no meaning at all, which was the only way she could say them.

Two rows back, Seth was trying to catch her eye. They'd been in the same AP psych class all year, and he'd shown up in a suit he'd clearly borrowed from his older brother, the sleeves too long, his collar wrong. When she'd turned around during the second hymn, he had whispered, "You okay?" and she had nodded, and then he had done something terrible, which was to smile at her, quickly, a reflex of friendship, before he caught himself and pressed his mouth flat.

After the service, in the basement hall where the coffee and sandwiches were, Payton found him by the punch bowl, holding a cup he wasn't drinking. "I need to tell you something," he said, low, urgent. "And I don't want you to impugn my motives, or think I didn't love him, because I did, your grandpa taught me how to solder when we built that radio in tenth grade." He was talking fast, the way he did before a test he hadn't studied for. "But today at lunch, before I came here, Michael was telling me about the calc exam, and I laughed. Like actually laughed, at a joke about Mr. Suzuki's word problems, and then I remembered I was coming here and I felt like a monster. I should be wrecked. It's been four days and I'm still going to school and doing homework and I laughed."

Payton looked at him, at the borrowed suit and the cup of punch sweating in his hand, and something in her loosened. "Come here," she said, and led him past the casseroles to the folding chairs by the Sunday school bulletin board, where a construction-paper banner said HE IS RISEN in crayon.

The night before, she hadn't slept. Around three in the morning she'd been sitting at her laptop, not crying, feeling like her lack of crying was evidence of something, maybe culpability, maybe a hollowness in her that her grandfather had seen all along, and she had typed into the search bar: is it normal not to cry when someone dies. Most of what came up was junk, stages and steps and promises about how grief must proceed, and she'd almost closed the laptop. Then she'd found a study by a psychologist named George Bonanno, who had followed bereaved people over time, and what he found was not what the internet kept insisting. Resilience was common, his research said. Most people weren't destroyed by loss, and there were no mandatory stages that everyone had to pass through. She had read it twice, then three times, and then, for the first time since Tuesday, she had cried, briefly, with something almost like relief.

"It's real, what you're feeling," she told Seth now. "It's just not the only way to feel it." She pulled out her phone, found the tab still open, and held it out so he could read. He read slowly, his lips moving a little, and she watched his shoulders come down an inch at a time.

"I thought there was a script," he said finally. "Denial, anger, the whole staircase."

"Yeah, well." She took the phone back. "There isn't a staircase. There's just you, and the radio he helped you build, and however it comes out." She didn't tell him that she still wasn't sure whether her own steadiness was health or delay, whether the crying would arrive next week like a delayed train, whether that would be worse. She was honest enough with herself to admit she didn't know, and honest enough to let that be all right for now.

Her mother appeared at the top of the basement stairs, waving her up; the elderly neighbours were leaving and Payton had promised to walk Mrs. Okafor to her car. She stood, smoothed her black skirt, and touched Seth once on the shoulder. "Eat a sandwich," she said. "Grandpa would want the sandwiches eaten." Then she climbed the stairs into the afternoon light, where the organ music was still drifting from the sanctuary, thin now, and Mrs. Okafor was waiting at the door with her cane and her handbag clutched in both hands, saying, "He was a good man, your grandfather. Now, where did I leave my car?"

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under the legal rule called contra proferentem, used in many jurisdictions, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it.
story:
Alicia had been staring at the waiver for four minutes when Drew leaned over her shoulder at the gym front desk and read the line aloud. "Participant assumes all liability for injury arising from use of the facility." He said it the way he said most things, like a joke she hadn't gotten yet. Behind the desk, Mr. O'Brien, who owned the place and had coached her brother's wrestling team for a decade, was sorting keys into a drawer without hurrying anyone.

"I want to climb," Alicia said. The new wall rose at the back of the gym, tall and gray, its handholds scattered like a chart of some montane range reduced to colored plastic. She had wanted it since September, when the semester's stress had started sitting in her shoulders like a stone. But her mother had signed the permission slip for the climbing course with a ballpoint pen pressed so hard it tore the paper, and afterward had said, read it first, all of it.

"Then sign it," Drew said. "Everyone signs it."

"Everyone signs it without reading it." She flattened the page against the counter. The trouble was one sentence near the bottom, a condition in smaller type: "Members under 18 must have a waiver on file." On file. Not signed by a parent, not countersigned, just on file. Her mother worked until seven and drove forty minutes to get here, and the course started Tuesday.

"Mr. O'Brien," she said. "This line about under-18 waivers. Does my mom have to sign it in person?"

He came over, wiped his hands on a towel, and squinted. "Waiver on file. Yeah. She has to sign."

"But it doesn't say that. It says on file. What if I sign it and she confirms by phone? Or what if I sign it as her?" She heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "It says member assumes liability. It doesn't say the member's parent assumes it. If I'm the member, and I'm the one who signed, then I assumed it."

"You can't sign for your mom," he said, but slower, reading the sentence again.

Damian arrived with his gym bag and dropped it on the scale. "What are we fighting about?"

"The contract," Alicia said. "It's badly written and I want to know who that hurts."

She had spent Sunday evening on the laptop in the kitchen, past the forums and into a legal site for consumers, reading about phone companies and gym memberships and people who had argued over a single unclear line. She'd found a rule there with a long Latin name, and she'd written it on the back of a receipt, and now she took the receipt out of her pocket.

"Under a rule called contra proferentem," she said, "an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it." Damian raised his eyebrows. "You wrote this," she told Mr. O'Brien. "You, or whoever printed it for you. So if the sentence is unclear, it's unclear in your favor to fix, not mine to suffer for. The reading has to go my way, or at least the doubt does. That's how it works in a lot of places."

Mr. O'Brien rubbed the back of his neck. "Where'd you learn that?"

"A phone company tried it on somebody. The somebody won." She hadn't meant to historicize it, to turn it into a story with heroes, but it was hard not to; the website had made the rule feel like a small sword handed down to ordinary people. "I'm not trying to win, though. I'm trying to climb Tuesday. My mom can't come in before seven any night this week."

The gym went quiet enough that she could hear the rope by the wall creak in the vent's draft. Mr. O'Brien read the sentence a third time, mouthing it.

"Okay," he said at last. "Phone confirmation won't do. That part's not ambiguous to me, whatever the paper fails to say, because a waiver that isn't witnessed isn't worth anything if you get hurt. But the form can be mailed, signed, mailed back. And I'll rewrite the line so the next kid doesn't stand here doing case law at my front desk." He pulled a pad toward him and started drafting, crossing out "on file" and writing something longer above it. "Consideration for your trouble: you get Tuesday. Call your mother from here."

Alicia didn't fully believe the second part, that doubt always flowed toward the weaker party, that a rule on the internet would hold up in an actual room with actual people. Maybe it only worked when someone like Mr. O'Brien decided to be reasonable. She dialed, and her mother's voice came through small and suspicious, then, hearing Mr. O'Brien's voice on the extension, easier. A form would go out tomorrow. Yes, she'd read it. Yes, all of it.

"That's the denouement," Damian said, leaning on the counter. "Everything after this is just paperwork."

Mr. O'Brien tore the draft off the pad and handed it to her. "Read it back to me," he said. "You're better at this than the lawyer I didn't pay."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
story:
The calves had gotten into the lower pasture again, and Owen found himself standing in the doorway of the barn explaining DNA to a boy who mostly wanted to talk about trucks. Ismael had come out to the farm because Mr. Janssen paid ten dollars an hour for fence work, and fence work was better than his uncle's shop, and that was the whole of his reasoning. Owen, on the other hand, had spent three weeks with a borrowed biology textbook, reading it in the hayloft during breaks, and the reading had gotten tangled up with the place itself until he could not look at a seed corn without thinking about instructions being read out.

"You're doing that thing again," Ismael said, hauling a post onto his shoulder. "That staring thing."

"I'm thinking about transcription."

"Bless you."

"Seriously." Owen followed him along the fence line, boots sinking where the irrigation had made the ground soft. "Every cell in that corn, in that calf, in you, there's a copy of instructions. And when a cell divides, it copies the whole thing first. A teacher at my old school called it semiconservative, which sounds political but isn't."

Ismael set the post in its hole and leaned on the tamping bar. "Sounds like something you made up to sound smart."

Owen had wondered, at first, whether he had it wrong. The textbook had been careful about it, and he'd read the page four times in the loft with dust burnishing the afternoon light gold around him, half convinced and half not. Was a copied molecule entirely new, built from scratch like a photograph of a photograph? Or was something of the original carried forward? He had wanted it to be the first one, he realized, because the first one was cleaner. A perfect fresh copy. The second idea was stranger and, somehow, more moving: that the old molecule splits down the middle and each half keeps serving, each half paired with a newly built partner.

"It's half old," he said now. "Each new double helix keeps one strand from the original and pairs it with one strand that's newly built. So after copying, you've got two molecules, and every one of them is half the original."

Ismael stopped tamping. "Half of it is the actual one from before? The same one?"

"That's what semiconservative means."

"Huh." Ismael squinted at the fence, then at the pasture, then at nothing in particular. He was quiet for a while, which was unusual enough that Owen waited. "So it's like when my grandfather's house got added onto. They kept the original wall."

Owen considered this. "Sort of. Except it happens twice, and both halves keep a wall." He was aware this was not quite a perfect analogy and said so, and Ismael shrugged and said analogies were like fences, good enough if they held.

Mr. Janssen drove out at four with feed and a montane hay map he'd picked up from a grower upcountry, and while he unloaded he asked what they'd accomplished, and Ismael, to Owen's surprise, said, "Owen taught me that DNA is half old when it copies. Semiconservative." He pronounced it carefully, like a word he'd decided to keep. Mr. Janssen looked at Owen over the tailgate and said only, "That right?" in a tone that could have been a question or a test.

There had been a day, two years ago, when Owen could not have answered that tone. He'd stood in a classroom after a test he'd failed and a teacher had said he wasn't applying himself, and he had believed her, because he had nothing better to believe. The farm had fixed that by accident. Mr. Janssen never explained anything twice; you watched the grafting, or the farrier's work, or the way he read weather off the western ridge, and you either noticed or you didn't. Owen had turned out to be a noticer, an autodidact by circumstance if not temperament, teaching himself from library books and from the animals themselves, and somewhere in that he had stopped trusting people who told him what he was.

"That's right," he said. "Half the original is kept in each copy. One old strand, one new one, in each of the two molecules."

Mr. Janssen nodded once and went on unloading feed, which was how he ended most conversations that mattered.

Later, at the fence's far corner, Ismael said his actual plan was to save enough by September for a down payment on a truck with a plow, so he could take winter contracts and stop working for other people entirely. He said it while staring at the tailgate latch, not at Owen, the way people say the things they mean most. Owen asked whether the truck would be new or used, and Ismael said used, definitely used, because a truck with some of the original still in it ran truer. Then he laughed at himself, and Owen laughed too, and neither of them said what they were both thinking.

The sun dropped behind the ridge and they stacked the last posts in the dark. Owen's hands smelled of creosote and his shoulder ached from the tamping bar, and he kept turning the molecule over in his mind, the way it split and rebuilt and carried half of what it was into everything that came after. He wondered whether the instructions for making protein, the transcription and translation he'd read about, worked the same way in the corn and the calves and Ismael's future truck, or whether some things got built from nothing at all.

"Corn next year comes from this corn," Mr. Janssen said from the barn door, as if he'd heard the question. "Half of it does, anyway."

"How do you know that?" Owen called.

Mr. Janssen tipped his hat back. "Grew up on this farm. Ask the seed."

Owen picked up the last post and carried it toward the barn.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The first loaf came out of the community kitchen's oven looking like a brick with ambitions, and Ryder poked it with a finger and watched the crust spring back without giving anything away. His mother had asked him for bread, plain and simple, because the store on their street had closed and she worked doubles now. He had agreed, partly to be useful and partly because Mr. Siddiqui's Saturday class at the kitchen had enraptured him more than he wanted to admit, the way dough turned from paste to something alive under his hands.

He cut the loaf open on the scarred counter. Inside it was dense and crumbly, nothing like the open, holey crumb of the bread in Mr. Siddiqui's demonstration. He had mixed flour and water and salt and yeast, and he had kneaded it, or thought he had, maybe four minutes of pushing it around the counter while checking his phone. Chiara, who took the class with him and worked the Saturday shift washing dishes, leaned over the crumb and squinted at it.

"You didn't build it," she said. "It's still just flour and water holding hands loosely."

"What does that even mean?"

"Gluten," she said. "That's the thing you were supposed to build."

He turned the word over while he cleaned the counter. In class, Mr. Siddiqui had mentioned it once, in passing, the way he mentioned most things, and Ryder had been busy weighing flour and missed it. He knew the word from grocery aisles, from a classmate's lunch that came with warnings, from somewhere in the fog of a semester of immunology notes he'd skimmed for biology. It had never occurred to him that gluten was something a baker made rather than something a bag contained.

He found Chiara at the sink, her hands in the suds. "So what is it? Actually."

She shrugged, drying a bowl. "Honestly, Siddiqui said it in like one breath. The proteins in wheat, glutenin and gliadin. They're already in the flour, but they don't do anything until they get wet. When flour meets water, they link up and form gluten. That's it. That's the whole magic. Wet flour becomes a network."

"A network."

"Like a net. That's what holds the bread together. That's why it's chewy." She flicked suds at him. "And here's the part you skipped. The more you knead it, the stronger the network gets, and the chewier the bread comes out. You kneaded yours for what, a commercial break? So there was barely any net, and your bread fell apart into crumbs. Makes sense, right?"

It did make sense, and the sense of it arrived in his chest before it arrived in his head, the way answers sometimes did. He had thought kneading was ceremony, something bakers did because bakers had always done it. Instead it was construction. Every fold and push was doing something at a scale he couldn't see, to proteins he hadn't known were there, and the bread was the record of how long he had kept at it. His dense little brick wasn't a failure of luck. It was a transcript.

He started a second batch before the class ended, weighing the flour carefully this time. While it rested, Mr. Siddiqui drifted over and asked what he was making, and Ryder told him about the first loaf, the crumb that scattered when he pulled it apart. Mr. Siddiqui nodded toward the window, where the light was going amber over the parking lot and the walking trail beyond it that ran along the river. "Takes patience," he said. "Everything along that riparian path took a hundred years to look easy. Bread's the same idea, sped up."

Ryder kneaded the second dough for ten full minutes, then fifteen, timing it on his phone, which stayed face down and silent. The change came gradually and then all at once: the shaggy mass smoothed, then tightened, then began to push back against his palms like something with an opinion. He stretched a piece of it thin and could see light through it without it tearing. Chiara passed behind him, glanced at the windowpane of dough stretched between his fingers, and gave him a thumbs-up with a wet hand.

The second loaf came out at closing time, taller, hollow-sounding when he knocked its base, and he carried it home warm against his chest, up the hill and the two flights, and set it on the counter just as his mother came through the door. She tore off the end piece, still steaming, and chewed. "It's chewy," she said, eyebrows up. "Really chewy."

Ryder laughed. "That's on purpose. That part, anyway. Everything else I'm still figuring out."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen.
story:
The porch at his grandfather's house had one good chair and one wobbling table, and Brayden had claimed both by ten in the morning, spreading his notebook, the textbook, and a printed article he'd been meaning to collate with his own notes since Monday. The assignment was short: a one-page history to accompany the calculus unit, due to Mr. Clarke on Friday. He'd drawn the topic "the integral" out of a hat in class, which Nelly found hilarious, since she'd drawn "zero" and could finish her report in a paragraph. Anson had drawn "pi" and had already written two pages, mostly complaints.

The problem Brayden actually cared about was smaller than the report and larger than it at the same time. He could do the rectangle method. He could chop the area under a curve into slices, add them up, and watch the sum close in on a number as the slices got thinner. What he couldn't yet see was why anyone believed the number was real, why the area existed at all rather than just being approached forever, like a door nobody actually opened. His grandfather, who was inside watching a program about immunology and complaining at the television whenever the narrator oversimplified, had told him at breakfast that this was the difference between a boy who does sums and a man who does mathematics. Then he'd gone back to his eggs.

So Brayden read. He read the textbook's version first, which named the method after Bernhard Riemann and moved on to the notation, and then the printed article, which stopped him cold. Riemann had given his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen. Brayden read the sentence twice, then a third time, copying it into his notebook with the date circled. He had assumed the rectangles were ancient, something the Greeks had settled, and finding out that the definition was barely older than the photograph of his great-great-grandmother on the hallway wall made the whole subject feel suddenly fragile, recently built, still warm.

"Grandpa," he called through the screen door, "when did you learn this stuff?"

His grandfather turned the television down. "Nineteen fifty-eight. Why?"

Brayden did the subtraction in the margin without thinking, then crossed it out, because it wasn't for the report. A hundred and four years between the definition and the man in the kitchen, and then sixty-some more to him, and each generation handing it down slightly dented. He wondered whether Riemann, standing in Göttingen hoping to qualify for a lectureship, had any image of a boy on a porch a hundred and seventy years later, arguing with the idea on his behalf.

Anson biked over after lunch and sat on the porch steps eating chips with a profligate disregard for the textbook, leaving grease prints on the cover. "You're overthinking it," Anson said, looking at Brayden's pages of rectangles getting thinner and thinner. "You just do the limit and it works. My brother says the AP only wants the procedure."

"That's what bothers me," Brayden said. "It works before you understand it. Everything in this class works before you understand it. Then you get to one problem where it doesn't work and you find out you never knew anything."

Anson shrugged and ate another chip. Nelly texted a photo of her finished report, one paragraph on zero, and the message "some of us are free." Brayden set the phone face down and went back to the pages.

Here was the thing he could not yet say out loud, though he wrote it in the margin and then half-scribbled it out. The rectangles were honest in a way the polished answer wasn't. Each rectangle was wrong, provably wrong, overhanging the curve or falling short of it, and yet the sum of all those wrong answers leaned toward something exact. He had always thought truth and error were opposites, that being right meant never being wrong, and now this method took a thousand small errors and made of them one true number. His grandfather's version, the man who does mathematics, seemed to want certainty at the end. But maybe the definition itself, the one Riemann submitted in 1854 to qualify at Göttingen, was really a way of agreeing to be wrong on purpose, at scale, with discipline. Brayden didn't know which position he held. He wrote both in his notebook and left a line between them.

At four o'clock his grandfather came out with two glasses of iced tea, set one on the wobbling table, and stood looking at the pages of narrowing rectangles. He didn't explain anything, which Brayden was grateful for, and after a while he said, "Your grandmother used to sit out here with her ledgers. Same look on her face as yours."

"There's a look?"

"There's a look," his grandfather said, and went back inside, leaving the screen door to clap shut behind him.

Brayden drank the tea, typed the sentence about 1854 and Göttingen into the report, and then, on a fresh page, began drawing the curve again, slicing it thinner than before.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data.
story:
The gym at the community center smelled of floor wax and old rubber, and Nevaeh had learned to love that smell the way you love a bus route you ride every day. Tuesdays and Thursdays she played point guard for the center's winter league team, a ragged squad of seniors and college freshmen coached by a retired electrician who believed, above all else, in the hot hand. If you made two in a row, you got the ball until you missed. That was the whole system.

Ryker, who sat the bench more than he played and kept a composition notebook of shot charts, thought the system was stupid. He said so during water breaks, in the flat voice he used for anything he considered obvious. "There's no hot hand," he told the team one Thursday in January, after the coach had ridden Emerick's streak for eleven straight possessions and lost them the game. "It's a fallacy. They proved it in 1985. If you flip a coin and it comes up heads, the next flip is still fifty-fifty. Same with shots."

The coach said the 1985 people never played ball. Emerick said Ryker should try shooting sometime instead of counting. Nevaeh said nothing, mostly because she was the one who had made the passes that fed Emerick's streak, and she wasn't sure whether the streak had been real or whether her passes had just been that good.

She found out differently the way she found out most things, sideways. Ms. Sinclair, who ran the center and kept a shelf of donated magazines and paperbacks in the lobby, was clearing it out for repainting, and Nevaeh helped her carry boxes on a Saturday because the center had become the place she went when home was too small. In one box there was a statistics magazine with a folded page, and on the folded page was a headline about streaks. She stood in the lobby with sawdust drifting in the window light and read it twice.

In 2018, she read, two economists, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo, showed that the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias, and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data. The same data. She read that part a third time. The notebook number Ryker carried around like scripture had been built on a cracked foundation, and the crack was invisible to everyone for thirty-three years, and the two economists had found it without a single bounce of a ball. She put the magazine in her jacket, and Ms. Sinclair, who saw everything and mentioned almost nothing, said only, "Take it, it's going to the recycling."

On Thursday she waited until Ryker was filling his water bottle. "That 1985 study," she said. "In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed it had a statistical bias, and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data." She'd practiced the sentence on the bus so it would come out like a fact and not like a trap. Ryker looked at her the way he looked at a shot chart with a column miscounted.

"That's not how probability works," he said, but she watched him do the thing she'd watched him do in math class, which was not defend his position but test it, quietly, behind his eyes, the whole walk home. He was like that: his certainty was ductile, it bent before it broke. It was one of the reasons she liked him even when he was unbearable.

The twist came at the last practice of the season. Ryker showed up with the magazine itself, borrowed from her locker with a note that said only "please," and he'd marked the article with three different pens. "It's real," he said. "The hot hand. I ran the numbers on our games and I can't tell, our sample's garbage, but theirs isn't." And then the coach, who had overheard exactly enough, put Ryker in the scrimmage and told Nevaeh to give him the ball, and Ryker, who had spent the winter insisting that streaks were a story people told themselves, made three shots in a row. He stood at the arc after the third one with his hands open at his sides, like a man who had been handed something and couldn't decide whether to keep it.

Nevaeh brought him the ball for the fourth. She did it partly because the coach's system was hers now too, and partly because she believed, on evidence, that it might work; but she also knew the fourth could miss for a hundred reasons no study would ever amortize across enough games to matter, and that her belief and her doubt were both hers to hold at once. That felt less like a contradiction than like the truth about everything she'd ever cared about. She would not have called her old certainty about anything solipsism, she didn't have the word, but she had begun to notice when a belief was mostly a mirror. Ryker caught the pass, spun the ball once in his hands, and set his feet at the arc.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
My grandfather's guitar had sat in the hallway closet for as long as I could remember, and I told everyone I picked it up because it was just there, which was mostly true, except that "just there" took me three days of noticing before I reached for it. I was sixteen. I told myself sixteen was practically the same as starting young, the way you tell yourself a lot of things at that age, and I practiced in the back room with the door shut so nobody could hear how bad I was.

Aaliyah found out about it on a Tuesday, when she came over to return a book and heard me through the wall. "How long have you been playing?" she asked, and when I said two weeks she laughed, not unkindly, but enough that I felt it in my hands. She said her cousin had started guitar at seventeen and quit, because of the ten thousand hours. "Too many hours," she said. "You'd have to practice for years before you're even good. Starting now, it's pointless." I said something dismissive about how I wasn't trying to be good, which was the first thing in this story that wasn't true.

That night I looked it up, and there it was, in Malcolm Gladwell's book Outliers, from 2008, the ten thousand hour rule he'd made famous. Ten thousand hours to master something. I did the arithmetic twice on the back of my grandfather's electricity bill: three hours a day for nine years, or one hour a day for twenty-seven. I would be forty-three. My grandfather had been dead for two years by then, and the guitar's provenance was thin, just a label inside the sound hole and my mother's vague memory of him playing it at a party once, decades ago. An instrument with almost no history, inherited by a boy with no head start. I almost put it back in the closet.

I didn't, though, and I want to be clear that it wasn't stubbornness. I'd decided it was a kind of experiment, cerebral and detached, a project I could write about later, maybe for a college essay, which shows you how honestly I was approaching it. I kept a notebook of my practice times and told myself the numbers meant nothing to me. I was counting them, obviously. I counted everything.

In November I hit a wall with the F chord, the barre, and I spent a week pressing the same shape until my fingertips split, and the whole thing felt like evidence for Aaliyah's cousin. Jakob, who sat behind me in chemistry, told me he'd read something. "You know Ericsson said the hours thing is wrong," he said, leaning over my notebook at lunch. "The guy the rule came from. He said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours." I asked what quality meant and Jakob shrugged, because he was the kind of person who read things once and let them go, and I was the kind who couldn't.

So I stopped counting hours and started counting mistakes, which sounds wise now but felt miserable then. I slowed everything down until the song I was playing was unrecognizable, and when I got a passage clean three times in a row I moved on, and when I didn't I stayed. Some evenings this worked. Other evenings I caught myself grinding through sloppy repetitions just to feel the time pass, and I couldn't always tell which kind of practice I was doing, and no one was standing behind me to say. That was the part nobody wrote a book about, I thought, the part where you're alone with your own bad judgment.

By spring I could play four songs all the way through, and I played one for my mother in the kitchen, and she cried, which I had not expected and did not know what to do with. I told Aaliyah I was still terrible, fishing, and she said, "Yeah, but you're less terrible than October," and Jakob asked whether I'd hit ten thousand hours yet and I said the number didn't matter, and then had to admit, when he raised an eyebrow, that I actually didn't know anymore whether it mattered. Maybe the hours mattered and the quality mattered and they were braided together in some way I couldn't separate. I was honest about that, at least. It was the only thing I was fully honest about, if you don't count the hours, and you shouldn't, because I counted them all.

The guitar stayed in the back room that summer, out of the closet now, leaning against the window where the light came through in the late afternoon. I practiced while my mother cooked and while the neighbor's dog barked and while Aaliyah texted me songs she said I should learn. My fingers had hardened into something useful. I would never know if I was doing it the right way, and I had stopped pretending that bothered me, mostly.

The last day of August I sat on the back step with the guitar and played the F chord, clean, four times, and then a fifth.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The screen door at her grandmother's house had a trick to it, a lift and a shove at the same time, and Amelia still got it wrong on the first try. She carried her duffel in past the kitchen, where her grandfather sat with the newspaper folded to the crossword and a paperback splayed open beside it, its spine cracked from rereading. Swim gear smelled up the bag no matter what she did about it. She dropped it by the cellar stairs and went to wash her hands.

"You're early," her grandfather said, not looking up.

"Practice got cut. Coach had a meeting." She dried her hands on the towel with the faded roosters on it and stood at his shoulder, reading the crossword clues upside down out of habit. Seven letters, "wisdom." She could never tell him the answer because he liked finishing them himself, so she only said "sagacity" under her breath, and he grunted, wrote it in, and turned the page of his paperback.

Jana was coming at four. They had planned it for a week, a Tuesday between the morning double and the Wednesday meet, and Amelia had spent the drive out here composing and abandoning sentences. The relay exchange had gone badly twice at the last meet, and afterward, in the locker room, one of the older girls had said, "Jana, you always mess this up," and the room had gone quiet the way rooms do when everyone agrees and no one will say so. Amelia had said nothing. That silence sat in her like a stone.

She got herself a glass of water and sat across from her grandfather. "Do you and Grandma ever fight?"

He set down his pen. "Fifty-one years. What do you think?"

"About what?"

"Dishes. The thermostat. Her sister." He tapped the paperback. "There's a psychologist in here, Gottman. He distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character." He said it plainly, the way he recited phone numbers, and went back to the crossword.

Amelia turned the glass in her hands. So "you never close the dishwasher" was one thing and "you're a slob" was another, and the line between them was thin enough to cross without noticing, in a locker room, at four in the afternoon at a kitchen table. The older girl hadn't said Jana missed the exchange twice. She had said always, which wasn't even true, and mess up, which was Jana entire, her nerves, her lateness, everything she was rather than anything she'd done. Amelia could see how the first version might be workable and the second might not, though she wasn't sure yet whether knowing the difference would make her any braver.

Jana arrived at ten past four, hair still wet from her own shower, and her grandmother fed them leftover lemon cake on the porch whether they wanted it or not, which they did. Afterward they walked down to the pond behind the garden, past the apple tree her grandmother had never let anyone expropriate for firewood, dead branches and all, because her own father had planted it. Jana skipped a flat stone and it went twice and sank.

"I know why you wanted to hang out," Jana said. She said it to the water, not to Amelia.

"Partly to hang out. Partly the exchange."

"You're going to tell me I always mess it up."

"No." Amelia picked up her own stone and weighed it, a small delay she allowed herself. "That's not what I'm going to say, and it isn't even what happened. You left early on the last two exchanges. First one at the meet, and the one in time trials." She watched a dragonfly stitch the surface of the pond. "When you go early, I'm not there yet, so we lose the touch. If you wait a half count longer, I think we've got it."

Jana threw another stone without skipping it. The reeds ticked against each other in the wind. "A half count."

"Maybe less. Coach has video."

"You sound like Coach."

"I sound like someone who watches the video." Amelia felt the strangeness of it, that being specific could feel colder than being cruel had, like handing Jana a form to sign. She thought about her grandfather's book, the complaint that stays a complaint only if you keep it nailed to the behavior, and how easy it would be for it to slide, one tired word, into something about who Jana was. She also thought that Jana hadn't said no, hadn't walked up the hill, was still standing there turning a stone over in her hand.

"Everyone else just says I'm flaky," Jana said finally. "Beau told me the team thinks I don't care."

"Do you care?"

"You know I care. I'm here on my day off."

"Then that's what I'll say, if anyone asks. That you were here, and we worked on the exchange." Amelia skipped her stone, and it went three times, then four, the last hop so faint it barely counted. Jana laughed, and threw hers, and for a while they just did that, seeing who could get more, not keeping score out loud.

On the walk back up, her grandfather was taking the dead branches off the apple tree after all, one small concession at a time, and he asked how it went. Amelia said, "We worked on the timing," and he nodded and handed her a branch to stack. Whether the half count would hold under the noise of a meet, whether the older girl would find some new way to say the old thing, Amelia couldn't promise any of it. She stacked the branch on the pile and reached for the next one.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A first-person narrator can report only what that one character sees, knows or chooses to say, while a third-person omniscient narrator can reveal any character's thoughts.
story:
The bell over the door of Second Leaf Books had a small crack in it, so it rang flat, and Charlie had learned to hear the difference between customers and wind. She came in at four with her bag heavy on one shoulder, the novel in it weighted like contraband. Ms. Hernández looked up from the register, saw the paperback's bent corner sticking out of the zip, and nodded toward the back table without a word.

Arnaud was already there, three books open in front of him, and Saige arrived two minutes later with two coffees and one straw. "Essay's due tomorrow at nine," Saige said, sliding a cup across the table. "Eight a.m. if we want Ms. Hernández to print it for us." The shop's old printer only ran before nine, when the morning light through the front windows let you see the paper tray. That was the deadline, and Charlie felt it sitting on her sternum like a palm.

The problem was the novel itself. Its narrator, a man named Rivas, told the story of a summer at his cousin's vineyard, and everything he said was plausible, generous, slightly self-mocking.
