But on page ninety he described a dinner he could not possibly have attended, because another character had already told him, on page sixty, that he was in the city that night. Charlie had found it at one in the morning and lain awake turning it over. "He lies," she said. "Not big lies. Small ones, and then one big one."

Arnaud pushed one of his books toward her. It was his own notebook, not a novel, a story he'd been drafting, and he wanted her to read it. "The narrator's a hedonist," he said. "Everything's wine and sunlight, no consequences. I want her to be charming and wrong." He'd been writing it since spring, and there was a contest, closing date tomorrow, that he'd only enter if someone he trusted confirmed the narrator worked. So the wants stacked on the table like the books: Charlie's essay, Saige's coffee going cold, Arnaud's pages.

Saige flipped to the dinner scene and read it twice. "Rewrite it," she said. "That's what I did for the exam. Take the same scene and put it in someone else's head, and you see exactly what changes." She said it as if it were nothing, a trick she'd once used, but Charlie felt something shift. She opened her notebook, wrote the dinner scene again from the cousin's perspective, third person, and stopped almost immediately. The cousin knew things Rivas never said. She knew the money was gone. She knew why Rivas mentioned the city.

"A first-person narrator can only report what that one character sees, knows, or chooses to say," Charlie said slowly, enunciating each phrase as though testing a floorboard. "And a third-person omniscient narrator can reveal any character's thoughts." In her rewrite, the reader learned, in one paragraph, what Rivas had spent two hundred pages withholding: that the whole summer was a debt, and the narrator was the debt. The lie on page ninety stopped being a flaw and became the point. Rivas had known the reader would catch him, eventually, and had counted on being liked first.

Then the twist, which came quietly. Arnaud read her rewrite over her shoulder, then looked at his own notebook, then closed it. "Mine doesn't do that," he said. "My narrator's lying to me, not to the reader. I believed her." He turned to a page near the middle and showed them a line the narrator said about her mother, a virulent little remark about the woman's selfishness, and Saige, who knew Arnaud's actual mother from three years of shared lunches, said nothing at all, and her saying nothing said everything. Arnaud sat back. "I can't fix it by tomorrow."

"Then don't enter this round," Ms. Hernández said from the register, where she had been listening the way she always listened, pretending to count stock. "The contest runs twice a year. The essay runs once." Charlie looked at the clock above the poetry shelf. It was six. She had three hours, a thesis she now believed, and a paragraph of rewrite that proved it. She also had a friend whose story needed the same surgery she'd just performed on Rivas, and no time to perform it. Both things were true, and she could only carry one home tonight.

She wrote the essay fast after that, the pen keeping pace with the argument, and at eight the next morning they stood by the printer while it ground through her pages, smelling faintly of hot dust. Arnaud held his notebook against his chest. "Next term," he said. "I'm rewriting her from the mother's point of view first, then back. Then I'll know what she's hiding." The printer pushed out the last page and went quiet. Charlie squared the stack, and on her way past the shelf of used fiction she slid Rivas's novel out and turned it so the cracked spine faced forward, cover out, where someone new might pick him up and believe him.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Savannah had chosen the mall because it was neutral territory, halfway between her house and his, and because it offered exits in every direction. She'd told Arielle this at lunch, laying it out like a battle plan, and Arielle had laughed so hard she knocked over her water. Now Savannah stood by the fountain near the east entrance, watching coins glow on the blue tile, pretending to check a phone that had nothing on it.

He arrived four minutes late, holding two tickets to the indoor mini-golf course that wound through the old wing of the mall, past the somnolence of shuttered storefronts where the overhead lights had been turned off to save money. His name was not important yet, she decided, still new enough in her mouth that saying it felt like a claim she hadn't earned. "You ready?" he asked, and she said she was, which was only partly true.

They were tied going into the eighteenth hole, a plastic windmill with a gate that opened and shut on a timer. The whole game had been closer than she expected, and she had stopped performing somewhere around the fifth hole, stopped narrating herself. On the eighteenth he sank his shot through the gate on the first try, which meant she had to match it to force a tiebreaker. Her heart was going hard enough that she could feel it in her wrists.

She made the putt. The windmill's blades swept past with a sound like a slow fan, and the ball dropped, and he raised both fists and shouted something the nearby shoppers turned to look at. Her hands were shaking. Not her chest, her actual hands, and something in her stomach was fizzing like a dropped soda, and she thought, distinctly, I feel something for this person, and then, less distinctly, or do I.

They went to the arcade afterward because the tiebreaker had to wait for the crowd to clear, and near the change machine she found Arielle, who worked weekends at the pretzel stand. Arielle raised an eyebrow at the boy, then at Savannah, then dragged her two steps away by the sleeve while he fed a dollar into a claw machine. "So how's it going," Arielle said, not really asking. Savannah told her about the eighteenth hole, the shaking hands, the fizzing.

"Oh, that's textbook," Arielle said, grinning. "We just did this in psych. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby." Savannah said that Arielle had just ruined possibly the best moment of her month, and Arielle said she was welcome, and went back to her pretzels.

But the word followed Savannah back across the arcade carpet, glittering under the black lights. Misattribution. She watched the boy win a stuffed frog from the claw machine on his third try and hold it out to her, and she took it, and she understood that the word cut both ways. If excitement could be mistaken for attraction, then a feeling she couldn't locate might be real or might be adrenaline, and there was no instrument for telling them apart. She could distrust the fizzing. She could also, she realized, standing there with a frog under her arm, decide that the distrust itself was a kind of answer, and she didn't want that either, because a boy who shouted at a windmill with his whole chest was not nothing, and pretending otherwise would be its own misattribution.

The tiebreaker hole was empty when they got back. The windmill turned its sullen, mechanical circuit, gate opening, gate closing, keeping its own time. He teed off first and missed by a centimeter, and groaned, and laughed at himself, and she stepped up to the ball. Her heart was still fast. She let it be fast. She could not say what it was, and she was, for once, not going to pretend she could. She squared her shoulders and putted through the gate.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Quran, in Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, exempts people who are ill or travelling from fasting during Ramadan, directing them to make up the same number of days later.
story:
The limestone headstone had a sedimentary grain to it, thin bands of grey laid down over ages, and Laura traced one band with her finger while her grandmother knelt in the grass beside her grandfather's plot and murmured the quiet words she always murmured here. It was the second Friday of Ramadan. Laura had come straight from debate practice, her file box still in the trunk of the car, and she had not eaten since before dawn.

"He would have liked that you're arguing about religion," her grandmother said, brushing cut grass from the stone. "He argued with the imam every Eid and then shook his hand."

"It's not really about religion," Laura said. "The resolution is whether ancient religious rules still apply in modern life. I have to build the case both ways and use the texts themselves. Mr. Morales says if we quote only commentators we lose points, we have to go to the source."

Her grandmother looked at her for a long moment, the way she did when Laura said something that was true and also beside the point. "And you are fasting."

"I am. Except." Laura stopped. On Thursday the team list had gone up: qualifiers were in Dallas, a four-hour drive, the weekend after next. Emersyn had texted her a screenshot with eleven exclamation points, and Payten had already claimed the window seat. Laura had read the message twice and then put the phone face down on the cafeteria table and finished her chemistry homework, and she had not mentioned it to anyone at home.

She mentioned it now, kneeling in the grass, her knees damp through her jeans. Her grandmother didn't answer right away. Instead she asked Laura to fetch the Quran from the car, the small one with the cracked spine that lived in the door pocket, and when Laura brought it back she said, "Read the verse about the fast. Al-Baqarah. You know the one I mean, you memorized it in fourth grade for the recitation contest."

Laura found it, Surah 2, and read the Arabic under her breath and then the English translation printed alongside it. The words said the month of Ramadan was the one in which the Quran was sent down, and that whoever among you was ill or on a journey should fast the same number of days later. She read it again. The cemetery around them was holding its noon stillness; a maintenance mower droned somewhere beyond the hedge, and a cardinal landed on the nearest headstone, a stranger's name she'd never read.

"Same number of days later," Laura said. "So it's in the text itself. Not a scholar's opinion, not a modern accommodation. The rule carries its own exception."

"It always did," her grandmother said. "Your grandfather travelled for work, those years at the plant in Houston. He made up his days after." She said it plainly, without weight, the way she said most things, and Laura understood that this was not a lecture but an offering: here is the verse, here is a man you knew, here is what he did.

But Laura had learned enough in debate to distrust neat closure, and something in her resisted anyway. The trip was only four hours by car; she would be sitting in a hotel, not walking a desert road. She could eat quietly at dawn and after dark and fast through the rounds. Plenty of classmates' parents took the strict view, and Mr. Morales would not care either way, and the resolution she had to argue was precisely this question, whether a rule from the seventh century still binds a life like hers, and she did not want her answer to be whatever was convenient. She wanted it to be considered. She said some of this out loud, kneeling there, and her grandmother listened without correcting her, which was its own kind of permission.

"Then argue it both ways on Saturday," her grandmother said, standing stiffly and brushing off her long skirt. "And argue it one way in your own life. They are not the same debate."

"That's such a debater thing to say," Laura said, and laughed, and her grandmother laughed too, a short surprised sound, and pulled her up by the wrist.

That night Laura sat at her desk with the file box open and the small Quran beside it. She wrote on one index card the case that the exemption itself proved the rule's durability, a law that anticipated travel and illness had never needed modernizing, and on another card the case that a rule requiring make-up days was a rule nonetheless, a debt to be paid, not a freedom. Between the two cards she set a blank one and left it blank. Her grandmother's voice at the graveside had cauterized one small fear, the fear that asking the question was itself a failure of faith, but the question remained, and she was beginning to think she could carry it to Dallas either way. At fajr she ate a piece of toast standing at the kitchen counter, and she set the travel dates beside the fasting days on her calendar, side by side, undecided.

Emersyn texted again: packing list? Laura typed back, not sure yet, and turned off the lamp.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: French economist Frédéric Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' argued that good economics must count the effects nobody sees.
story:
Ella had worked at the coffee shop on Marsh Street for eleven Saturdays, long enough to know that the espresso machine held its temperature like a small stubborn animal, some equilibrium it would not be pushed from. She wiped the steam wand and watched the door. Irene came in at four, as she always did before her evening class, and dropped her bag on the counter with a sound like a dropped book.

"Quiz on Monday," Irene said. "I haven't started." She pulled out a folder and flattened a photocopied syllabus against the counter, and Ella, leaning over to look, read the reading list upside down and then right side up when Irene turned it. Among the titles with dates beside them, one line caught her: Frédéric Bastiat, 1850, "That Which Is Seen, and That Which is Not Seen."

"What's that one mean?" Ella asked. She poured Irene's usual, a small drip coffee, milk on the side, because Irene believed specialty drinks were a scam.

"It's a French economist," Irene said. "The essay argued that good economics has to count the effects nobody sees." She said it in the flat voice she used for reciting things she did not yet own. "My teacher loves it. There will definitely be a question on it."

Eella turned the phrase over while she worked the register through the after-work rush, a man who wanted his latte extra hot, two women splitting a scone and arguing about a lease. Nobody sees. The window behind the counter gave onto the street, and past the glass she could see the music shop across the road, its window full of secondhand guitars. One of them, a sunburst acoustic with a scratched pickguard, had been there since September. She had gone in twice to hold it. Twice she had put it back down, because three hundred and forty dollars was most of what she had, and what she had was spoken for, though she had not told anyone what for, not even Irene.

Mr. Adebayo, who ran the newsstand two doors down, came in at six for his decaf. He had a way of standing at the counter as though it were a fence between two countries. "Busy today," he said, and then, nodding at Irene's folder, "Still studying money. Money and the things money hides." He took his cup and went out, and Irene groaned and put her head on the counter.

The shop emptied after seven. Ella mopped while Irene quizzed herself, whispering terms. Opportunity cost, Ella heard her say, the value of the next best alternative you give up when you choose. Ella stopped the mop. She had heard the phrase before, in school, and it had slid off her like water off the machine's steel back. Now it stuck. She thought of the guitar in the window, and she thought of the envelope in her sock drawer at home, and she stood with the mop dripping onto the tile while the sentence finished arranging itself.

Because here was the thing nobody saw: the envelope held two hundred and ninety dollars marked for the trip to the coast in July, the one Gabriel had organized, four days of cabins and a lake he would not stop describing. Her mother thought the money came from birthday cards. Ella had not corrected her. If she bought the guitar, the trip disappeared, and Gabriel would hear some excuse, and the excuse would be the thing that was seen, while the real trade stayed invisible in her sock drawer. Bastiat would have called it something, she was sure, some tidy French phrase for the cost you never show anyone.

Irene looked up. "You've been staring at that mop for a full minute."

"How much is your class," Ella said, "compared to working here tonight?"

Irene blinked. "I gave up a shift at the bookstore for this. I guess that's the cost. My teacher calls that opportunity cost." She bent back to her folder, and Ella felt something settle, not a resolution but a clearer shape, the way the river water she'd seen last summer had looked turbid from the bank and then, wading in, had turned out to be only waist deep.

She counted the drawer at closing. Two hundred and six Saturdays of wages sat in that sock drawer, or rather ten weeks of it, and the school system had somehow failed to inculcate in her the habit of counting what she wasn't buying. The numbers in her head would not finish. The guitar would be gone someday, sold to some kid with different arithmetic; the lake would come once, with Gabriel narrating the whole drive, and then everyone would scatter to colleges.

Irene packed up at eight. "Wish me luck," she said at the door.

Eella untied her apron, pulled her jacket from the hook, and stood a moment looking across the dark street at the music shop window, where the sunburst guitar caught the light of a passing bus and flared once, briefly, like something answering her. She zipped the jacket to the chin and went out the back to lock up, keys cold in her hand.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five 'filters', the first of which is the ownership of media by large corporations.
story:
The coffee shop on Marsh Street had one outlet near the window, and Felix had claimed it forty minutes ago for his laptop, his cold americano, and the copy of Manufacturing Consent that Ms. Yilmaz had pressed on him after third period. He was supposed to write a column for the student paper about the school board vote, due Sunday, and instead he was reading about propaganda models, which felt productive in the way that cleaning your room instead of doing homework feels productive.

"Is that a textbook?" Grant dropped into the chair across from him, uninvited, holding a muffin he had clearly bought only because it was the cheapest thing on the menu. "You look like a portrait of a sad graduate student."

"It's from 1988," Felix said. "Herman and Chomsky. They argued the news is shaped by five filters, and the first one is ownership, like when big corporations own the outlets." He turned the book so Grant could see the cover, as if the cover proved something.

"Filters like a water purifier?"

"Like whatever keeps some things out and lets other things through."

Grant bit his muffin and considered this with more seriousness than Felix expected. Then Nada arrived, still in her robotics club hoodie, and set down three napkins she had taken from the dispenser without asking, which was how she marked territory. She was the paper's editor, which meant she was the one who would tell Felix on Sunday that his column needed another draft.

"Read this part," Felix said, and slid the book toward her, finger holding a page. "Then tell me I'm crazy."

Nada read. Behind the counter, the espresso machine shrieked, and Ms. Yilmaz, of all people, appeared at the register in line with a tote bag, apparently getting coffee before the evening faculty meeting. She saw Felix and lifted two fingers off her cup in a salute that said, I see you reading, carry on. Felix felt obscurely surveilled, then annoyed at himself for feeling surveilled, since she was the one who had given him the book.

"Okay," Nada said. "So this is why you've been acting weird all week. You interviewed the coach Tuesday and kept asking who signs his paycheck."

"Because it matters." Felix pulled up a story on his laptop, the local coverage of the school board vote, the one about closing the field house for a year for renovation. "Look at the byline, then look at who owns that paper. It got bought last spring by the same developer whose name is on the proposal. They ran the developer's op-ed twice."

"Maybe they ran it because it's news," Grant said.

"Twice, Grant."

Nada pulled the laptop closer and began scrolling, which was how she sequestered a thing when she intended to keep it. Felix watched her expression change from skepticism to something more careful. "The story doesn't mention that the field house is where the swim team practices," she said slowly. "Six hundred kids. That's not in there anywhere."

"That's not a conspiracy," Grant said. "That's just bad reporting."

"Is there a difference?" Felix asked, and immediately regretted the way it sounded, like a poster in a dorm room. He tried again, quieter. "I'm not saying there's a room where men in suits decide what we're allowed to know. I'm saying the suits own the building, and the room is in the building."

Nada laughed at that, a short sound, surprising all three of them. Behind them Ms. Yilmaz collected her cappuccino and, passing their table, set down a bookmark she had apparently been carrying, a stiff paper one from the library. "Page forty," she said, and was gone before Felix could ask her anything.

"She sequesters information," Grant said. "It's like a disorder."

Felix found page forty. The chapter went on about the five filters, and he read a few paragraphs and then looked up, because the twist arrived not in the book but in his own head, arriving late and without apology: the developer's company did not own the local paper. He checked. The chain that owned it had been bought by a holding company, and the developer's name appeared nowhere in the ownership documents he could find. What he had, then, was a coincidence of coverage, a lazy reporter, a small town where the same twelve names appeared in every story for ordinary reasons. The op-ed had run twice because the op-ed editor was, by all accounts, disorganized, a man who once ran the same crossword two Fridays in a row.

"So you were wrong," Nada said, when he told them.

"I was wrong about the why," Felix said. "I think I was right that it's worth asking who owns things." He closed the laptop halfway. "I can write the column about the question instead of the answer."

"That's not a column," Grant said. "That's a shrug."

"It's a column with a byline and no owner," Nada said, and pushed the laptop back to him. "Write it. Deadline's Sunday at nine." She stacked her three napkins, took one anyway, and pocketed the bookmark.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
story:
Ashley spread the draft across the kitchen table at eleven at night, six scenes pinned in a row like laundry. The first took place at the lake in June, the second at the bus depot, the third in her grandmother's kitchen, and by the fifth she was writing a carnival she had only visited once and mostly invented. The play was supposed to be ten minutes long and it was about the entire summer her parents separated, which meant it was about everything and therefore, she suspected, about nothing.

She called Mikayla, who answered mid-yawn and did not sound sorry to be awake. "Read me your outline," Mikayla said, so Ashley did, scene by scene, and Mikayla was quiet for longer than a phone call usually allowed. Then she said, "Mr. Hu's handout. I have it right here. A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people." She read it flatly, like a weather report, and Ashley felt the six scenes slide off the table in her mind.

"One setting," Ashley said. "I have six."

"So pick one."

"That's like picking one photograph of a summer."

"Maybe that's what a ten-minute play is."

Ashley hung up and sat with the draft. The lake scene had her father in it, and the depot had her mother, and the kitchen had both, mid-argument, while Ashley's younger brother spilled juice on purpose to make them stop. The kitchen was the only scene where everybody was already in the room, and it was the scene she least wanted anyone to watch, because she had written it honestly and honesty was going to cost her something on a stage.

The next afternoon Abygael came over with her own script and two cans of lemonade, and they read for each other in the living room with the curtains open because Ashley's mother was home and would pass through occasionally, dusting things that were already clean. Abygael's play was subtle in a way Ashley envied: two girls folding laundry, never naming what they were arguing about, the whole rift carried in the fold of a shirt. Ashley's draft, by contrast, had people expatiating all over the place, announcing their feelings in paragraphs, and she heard it now with a stranger's ears.

"It's too much talk," Ashley said.

"Your kitchen scene isn't," Abygael said. "That one, nobody says what they mean. That's the one."

The problem was the kitchen scene was ten minutes by itself, but it needed the summer around it, or she had believed it did. She tried an experiment that evening, alone at the table while her mother watched television in the next room at low volume. She cut everything but the kitchen. Then she cut the brother, because few characters meant few, and gave the juice-spilling to her mother, a glass tipped sideways in the middle of a sentence, whether on purpose the audience would never know. The scene became ductile under her hands, bending where she pressed it, holding the shape of the whole summer inside one argument over a grocery list. What she lost was her father's face at the lake in June, which she had written beautifully and which now belonged to no play.

She showed Mr. Hu the revision two days later, and he read it without expression, which she had learned was his highest compliment. "You found the moment," he said, and handed it back, and asked only one question: whether she had asked her mother's permission. Ashley had not. She had assumed the argument, rearranged and disguised, was fiction enough.

Her mother read it Thursday night at the kitchen table, the actual table, in the actual kitchen, and Ashley stood by the sink pretending to wash a mug that was already clean. The pages turned slowly. When her mother finished, she set them down and smoothed the top sheet with one finger, the same gesture she used on the tablecloth before dinner.

"Your father never said that line about the groceries," her mother said.

"I know. I gave it to him."

"It was me who said it."

"I know," Ashley said. The mug went back under the tap, the water running over her wrists, and her mother picked up the pages again and turned to the second act, which was really only the second half of ten minutes, and began to read it a second time.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and cannot be removed simply because the legislature disagrees with them.
story:
The town hall smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and Sydney claimed a folding chair between Rhiannon and Hajar before anyone else could nab the good seats, the ones near the radiator. The agenda taped to the door listed storm drain repairs, the leash bylaw, and then, in Ms. Bouchard's tidy handwriting, "Youth Forum: How Leaders Get Hired and Fired." Sydney had come for the extra credit, which she admitted to no one, and because Ms. Bouchard had said whoever spoke best might get picked for the provincial youth parliament in the spring. That was the want, the real one, and she had practiced a speech in the shower that morning until the water ran cold.

The town sat on a narrow isthmus between the lake and the canal, which meant every meeting eventually became an argument about flooding, and tonight was no exception. Two men in hunting jackets debated a culvert for eleven minutes before the moderator pried the microphone back. Sydney used the time to peek at the notecard hidden in her sleeve, on which she had written, in her most confident print, "In our system the government falls when it loses the confidence of the House." She had copied it from a website at midnight and understood it roughly the way she understood her mother's research posters, the ones about phenotypic variation in sticklebacks, which was to say not at all.

When the youth forum finally started, Ms. Bouchard set out two chairs at the front like a talk show and said only, "Somebody be a prime minister. Somebody be a president. The rest of you are parliament and Congress, and you all despise your leader. Go." That was the whole instruction, which struck Sydney as either brilliant or lazy, possibly both.

Hajar volunteered to be the prime minister because, she said, her grandmother in Rabat had watched four governments come and go "like weather," and she wanted the practice. Rhiannon got the presidency, on the grounds that her aunt in Manila had once waited three years for an election no amount of complaining could move up. Sydney ended up in the legislature with everyone else, holding a paper sign that said, in crayon, NO CONFIDENCE.

The game went like this. Hajar proposed a terrible policy, a tax on anyone who clapped at meetings, and the legislature revolted instantly. Sydney leapt up waving her sign, feeling magnificent, and declared that the government had lost the confidence of the House and must resign. Hajar shrugged with impressive theatrical gloom and vacated her chair, murmuring something about packing her files. "In a parliamentary system that's it," she said, dusting off her hands. "My own party can even dump me between elections if I'm that bad."

Then Rhiannon took her turn. She proposed something even worse, mandatory karaoke on Sundays, and the legislature howled. Sydney stood again with her sign, invincible now, and demanded the president's resignation, and Rhiannon folded her arms and stayed exactly where she was. "Nope," she said cheerfully. "I was elected separately from you people, for a fixed term, and you can't remove me just because you disagree with me." Sydney waved the sign harder. Rhiannon examined her nails. The room began to giggle, and Sydney felt her shower-prepared confidence atrophy in real time, wilting like the lettuce in the school cafeteria.

"You're telling me she can just sit there?" Sydney said, appealing to the room, to Ms. Bouchard, to the radiator. "For years? Even though literally everyone hates the karaoke?" Rhiannon grinned and said, "Impeachment exists, but that's for crimes, not for being wrong," which Sydney filed away to Google later, because it sounded like the fine print on a warranty. Hajar called from the sidelines, "That's the trade, Syd. Your way gives you a sledgehammer and their way gives you a calendar." Sydney opened her mouth to argue and then, annoyingly, closed it, because the comparison was assembling itself in her head: one system makes removal easy and terms mushy, the other makes terms solid and removal nearly impossible, and the two of them were standing at opposite ends of that bridge arguing about who had the better view.

She raised her hand and, without the notecard, told the room what she had worked out: that she had walked in thinking her own system was simply more democratic because it was easier to fire a leader, and now she wasn't sure, because easy to fire also means easy to topple for petty reasons, and hard to fire means a government can ignore everyone for a fixed stretch. What she still didn't know, and said so out loud, was which failure mode she'd rather live with, and she suspected the honest answer depended on whether you trusted the voters or the legislators more, and she hadn't decided that yet either.

Ms. Bouchard wrote something on her clipboard. Rhiannon leaned over and whispered, "You just gave my aunt's president a compliment. She'd disown you." Then the moderator called the storm drain men back for a rematch, Hajar reclaimed her chair to pass judgment on the culvert as a deposed prime minister, and Sydney, feeling for her notecard, found her sleeve empty and realized she hadn't missed it. She reached for Rhiannon's crayon, and on the back of the NO CONFIDENCE sign printed, in careful letters, FIXED TERM.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension means a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around Gabriela's arm in the second-floor bathroom, the one nobody used after fourth period because the lights flickered. Annabelle watched the gauge climb and thought about her father's arm, three weeks ago, in a clinic hallway that smelled of disinfectant and old magazines. She had been the one holding his coat while the nurse wrapped the cuff, and she had seen the numbers before anyone said anything: 142 over 88.

"Ow, ow, it's cutting off my circulation," Gabriela said, which was the point, but Annabelle let it go. She was not really practicing on Gabriela for Gabriela's sake. In eight days she had to stand up in Mr. Weber's health class and demonstrate, for real credit toward the certification she needed for the hospital aide job next summer, how to take a blood pressure and then explain, in plain words, how diet and exercise could change it. The job was the want underneath everything, the thing she had not told her mother about yet because her mother would only say what she always said about Annabelle's plans, that they were fine, fine, as if the word were an injunction against hoping further.

"Top number first," Annabelle said, watching the needle settle. "One thirty-eight over eighty-two. You're alive." Gabriela laughed and rubbed her arm, and for a moment the bathroom felt almost easy, two girls and a borrowed cuff and the faucet dripping its small regular pulse.

What Annabelle could not get straight was the clinic. She kept circling back to it while Gabriela reapplied lip balm in the spotted mirror. The nurse had looked at 142 over 88 and said, almost offhand, "That's stage 2, we'll need to recheck." Stage 2. Annabelle had assumed, sitting there with the coat folded on her knees, that stage 2 meant both numbers were bad, that 88 had to be just as far gone as 142. But when she looked it up that night, hunched over her phone with the door shut, she found it worked differently. Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 140 or higher, or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher. Either one alone was enough. Her father's 88 was fine, not fine enough to save him from the label, but fine. The top number had done it all by itself.

"What's the face for?" Gabriela asked. Gabriela had her own reasons for being in this bathroom: Mr. Weber had hinted that he would pick one student from the class to help run the blood pressure station at the community health fair on Saturday, and Gabriela wanted that slot the way other people wanted prom. She had said so twice on the walk over, lightly, as if it were a joke, and Annabelle had not offered to step aside because the aide job and the fair could both be hers if she was good enough, and because friendship and ambition sat awkwardly on the same bench.

"It's my dad's numbers I keep thinking about," Annabelle said, and there it was, the fact she had been carrying like a stone since the clinic: not a stranger's reading, not a case study. Her father, who ate salted peanuts in front of the television and called walks "a waste of a good afternoon," had a top number of 142. She had let Gabriela believe she was studying a hypothetical patient all week. "One forty-two over eighty-eight," she said. "Three weeks ago."

Gabriela turned from the mirror. "Your dad?" The lights flickered, went steady, flickered again, and in the stutter of brightness Annabelle watched her friend's face change from confusion to something more careful. "And you didn't say."

"I didn't want it to portend anything," Annabelle said. "I wanted it to be arithmetic." That was the truth she had finally landed on, somewhere between the guideline page and this tile room: the number was a threshold, a line drawn by a committee she would never meet, and it did not by itself tell her whether her father's heart was a storm or just a door slamming in the wind. What she could do was smaller and more solid. She could learn the cuff. She could stand in front of Mr. Weber's class and say that aerobic exercise and less sodium could pull readings down, that it was slow and unglamorous and true, and then she could go home and say the same thing to her choleric father, who hated lectures worse than he hated vegetables, and watch what he did with it.

"Okay," Gabriela said slowly, unwinding the cuff from her own arm and holding it out. "Then practice on me again, but this time say the whole thing, the reading and the diet part, out loud, like he's in the room." The faucet dripped. Annabelle took the cuff, Velcro rasping, and pressed two fingers to the pulse inside Gabriela's elbow to find the right spot.

"Relax your arm," Annabelle said. "Dad, I'm going to tell you a number, and then I'm going to tell you what we can do about it."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state.
story:
The agenda item was number nine, which meant Connor had to sit through eight other things first, including a dispute about a fence that had already lasted two meetings. He had come to speak for the creek cleanup, whose funding was on the chopping block, and he had signed his name on the sheet at the door with the pen chained to the lectern, which did not strike him as a good omen for the kind of place this was.

Kiptyn had come with him, mostly for the entertainment value. On the bus over, they were still arguing about the debate their history class had been assigned: whether countries could ever actually agree on an environmental problem. Kiptyn said no, obviously not, and had brought a stack of examples, every one of them a failure. "Name one time it worked," he said, and Connor couldn't, which was the annoying thing. He had said he'd look it up, and hadn't, and now the not-knowing sat in him like a stone in a shoe.

The chamber smelled of carpet cleaner and burnt coffee. Mr. Ionescu, who taught chemistry at the high school and lived three doors down from the creek, was seated in the second row with a folder of photographs. He caught Connor's eye and held up the folder, then put a finger to his lips, as if the photographs themselves needed silence.

Item four ran long. A man at the microphone vilified the entire council, the mayor personally, and, somehow, the concept of roundabouts. The clerk read out the disbursement schedule for the quarter, a long dry recitation of numbers moving from one column to another, and Connor noticed that the cleanup's line, when it passed by, was small enough that he felt almost embarrassed to be defending something so cheap. That was the argument, he realized, writing it on the back of the agenda. Not that the creek was precious. That it was cheap.

Then item seven, and a surprise. A council member announced they had received written submissions, and the clerk unfolded a page and read a letter aloud. It was from Marco, who had promised Connor he would come and then, characteristically, had not. The letter said that Marco fished at the creek with his grandfather every June, that the grandfather had stopped coming two years ago because of the smell, and that Marco had kept going alone, and that he wanted the council to know the creek was worse this year than last, and that he was not a sentimental person, so they should take that seriously. The chamber was quiet after it. A few people laughed, the wrong kind of laugh, and then stopped.

When item nine arrived, the mayor was looking at the clock. Connor went up, knees slightlytraitorous, and made the cheap argument, and then, because the stone in his shoe was still there, he added that last night, finally, he had looked up the Montreal Protocol, the 1987 treaty that phased out ozone-destroying chemicals. "It was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state," he said, and heard his own voice go flat in the middle of the sentence, the way it did. Every single one. He said he wasn't claiming a creek was the ozone layer. He said only that when everyone was told the same thing by something they couldn't argue with, they had, once, all signed.

A council member with reading glasses asked whether the funding was a one-time cost or recurring, which was a reasonable question, and Connor didn't know the answer, and said so. Mr. Ionescu stood up from the second row without waiting to be called and said, "The photographs," and held the folder aloft like a witness brandishing evidence, and the mayor, who was not sanguine about interruptions, let it pass anyway, probably because it was late.

They continued the item to the next meeting, which meant nothing had happened and also that nothing had been killed. Outside, in the parking lot, Kiptyn said the Montreal Protocol thing was actually a decent point, said it grudgingly, as if paying a debt. Marco texted while they stood there: did they read my letter, did anyone laugh. Connor typed back that someone had laughed and then stopped, and that the stopping was the part that mattered.

Mr. Ionescu came out with his folder under his arm and paused beside them. "June," he said. "You'll want the photographs developed before June. After that the water drops and you can't see anything." He walked off toward his car, and Kiptyn looked at Connor, and Connor looked at the light coming on over the chamber door.
